Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There was a very good man, and a very bad man, called by the same name; for names commend us not to God, nor do they make men worse. Judas the apostle was never the worse, nor Judas the apostate ever the better, for being namesakes. But, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The evangelist carefully distinguishes between them; when he speaks of this pious Judas, he adds, <hi type="italic">not Iscariot.</hi> Take heed of mistaking; let us not confound the precious and the vile. [2.] What he said—<hi type="italic">Lord how is it?</hi> which intimates either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> the weakness of his understanding. So some take it. He expected the temporal kingdom of the Messiah, that it should appear in external pomp and power, such as all the world would wonder after. "How, then," thinks he, "should it be confined to us only?" <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ti gegonen</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">what is the matter</hi> now, that thou wilt not show thyself openly as is expected, that <hi type="italic">the Gentiles may come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising?</hi>" Note, We create difficulties to ourselves by mistaking the nature of Christ's kingdom, as if it were of this world. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> as expressing the strength of his affections, and the humble and thankful sense he had of Christ's distinguishing favours to them: <hi type="italic">Lord, how is it?</hi> He is amazed at the condescensions of divine grace, as David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18">2 Sam. vii. 18</reference>. What is there in us to deserve so great a favour? Note, 1. Christ's manifesting himself to his disciples is done in a distinguishing way-to them, and <hi type="italic">not to the world</hi> that <hi type="italic">sits in darkness;</hi> to the <hi type="italic">base,</hi> and not to the <hi type="italic">mighty</hi> and <hi type="italic">noble;</hi> to <hi type="italic">babes,</hi> and not to the <hi type="italic">wise</hi> and <hi type="italic">prudent.</hi> Distinguishing favours are very obliging; considering who are passed by, and who are pitched upon. 2. It is justly <hi type="italic">marvellous in our eyes;</hi> for it is unaccountable, and must be resolved into free and sovereign grace. <hi type="italic">Even so, Father, because it seemed good unto thee.</hi> <div eID="gen28089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28090" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ, in answer hereto, explains and confirms what he had said, <reference osisRef="John.14.23-John.14.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. He overlooks what infirmity there was in what Judas spoke, and goes on with his comforts. <div eID="gen28090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28091" type="x-p"/> [1.] He further explains the condition of the promise, which was loving him, and keeping his commandments. And, as to this, he shows what an inseparable connection there is between love and obedience; love is the root, obedience is the fruit. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Where a sincere love to Christ is in the heart, there will be obedience: "<hi type="italic">If a man love me</hi> indeed, that love will be such a commanding constraining principle in him, that, no question, he will <hi type="italic">keep my words.</hi>" Where there is true love to Christ there is a value for his favour, a veneration for his authority, and an entire surrender of the whole man to his direction and government. Where love is, duty follows of course, is easy and natural, and flows from a principle of gratitude. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> On the other hand, where there is no true love to Christ there will be no care to obey him: <hi type="italic">He that loveth me not keepeth not my sayings,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.24">v. 24</reference>. This comes in here as a discovery of those that <hi type="italic">do not love Christ;</hi> whatever they pretend, certainly those do not love him that believe not his truths, and obey not his laws, to whom Christ's sayings are but as idle tales, which he heeds not, or hard sayings, which he likes not. It is also a reason why Christ will not manifest himself to the world that doth not <hi type="italic">love him,</hi> because they put this affront upon him, not to <hi type="italic">keep his sayings;</hi> why should Christ be familiar with those that will be strange to him? <div eID="gen28091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28092" type="x-p"/> [2.] He further explains the promise (<reference osisRef="John.14.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">If a man thus love me, I will manifest myself to him. First, My Father will love him;</hi> this he had said before (<reference osisRef="John.14.21">v. 21</reference>), and here repeats it for the confirming of our faith; because it is hard to imagine that the great god should make those the objects of his love that had made themselves <hi type="italic">vessels of his wrath.</hi> Jude wondered that Christ should <hi type="italic">manifest himself to them;</hi> but this answers it, "If my Father love you, why should not I be free with you?" <hi type="italic">Secondly, We will come unto him, and make our abode with him.</hi> This explains the meaning of Christ's manifesting himself to him, and magnifies the favour. 1. Not only,<hi type="italic">I will,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">We will, I and the Father,</hi> who, in this, <hi type="italic">are one.</hi> See <reference osisRef="John.14.9">v. 9</reference>. The light and love of God are communicated to man in the light and love of the Redeemer, so that wherever Christ is formed the image of God is stamped. 2. Not only, "<hi type="italic">I will show myself to him</hi> at a distance," but, "<hi type="italic">We will come to him,</hi> to be near him, to be with him," such are the powerful influences of divine graces and comforts upon the souls of those that love Christ in sincerity. 3. Not only, "I will give him a transient view of me, or make him a short and running visit," but, <hi type="italic">We will take up our abode with him</hi> which denotes complacency in him and constancy to him. God will not only love obedient believers, but he will take a pleasure in loving them, will rest in love to them, <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zeph. iii. 17</reference>. He will be with them as at his home. <div eID="gen28092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28093" type="x-p"/> [3.] He gives a good reason both to bind us to observe the condition and encourage us to depend upon the promise. <hi type="italic">The word which you hear is not mine, but his that sent me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.24">v. 24</reference>. To this purport he had often spoken (<reference osisRef="John.7.16">ch. vii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.28">viii. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.44">xii. 44</reference>), and here it comes in very pertinently. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> the stress of duty is laid upon the precept of Christ as our rule, and justly, for that word of Christ which we are to keep is the Father's word, and his will the Father's will. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The stress of our comfort is laid upon the promise of Christ. But forasmuch as, in dependence upon that promise, we must deny ourselves, and take up our cross, and quit all, it concerns us to enquire whether the security be sufficient for us to venture our all upon; and this satisfies us that it is, that the promise is not Christ's bare word, but the Father's which sent him, which therefore we may rely upon.
entries.fc36df6fd86ff650294f380f7fb1278f4dd4420d: <div eID="gen28093" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Consolatory Discourse.</title> <div sID="gen28094" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> These things have I spoken unto you, being <hi type="italic">yet</hi> present with you. <hi type="super">26</hi> But the Comforter, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you. <hi type="super">27</hi> Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. <div eID="gen28094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28095" type="x-p"/> Two things Christ here comforts his disciples with:— <div eID="gen28095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28096" type="x-p"/> I. That they should be under the tuition of his Spirit, <reference osisRef="John.14.25-John.14.26">v. 25, 26</reference>, where we may observe, <div eID="gen28096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28097" type="x-p"/> 1. The reflection Christ would have them make upon the instructions he had given them: <hi type="italic">These things have I spoken unto you</hi> (referring to all the good lessons he had taught them, since they entered themselves into his school), <hi type="italic">being yet present with you.</hi> This intimates, (1.) That what he had said he did not retract nor unsay, but ratify it, or stand to it. What he had spoken he had spoken, and would abide by it. (2.) That he had improved the opportunity of his bodily presence with them to the utmost: "As long as I have been yet present with them, you know I have lost no time." Note, When our teachers are about to be removed from us we should call to mind what they have spoken, <hi type="italic">being yet present with us.</hi> <div eID="gen28097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28098" type="x-p"/> 2. The encouragement given them to expect another teacher, and that Christ would find out a way of speaking to them after his departure from them, <reference osisRef="John.14.26">v. 26</reference>. He had told them before that the Father would give them this other comforter (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">v. 16</reference>), and here he returns to speak of it again; for as the promise of the Messiah had been, so the promise of the Spirit now was, the consolation of Israel. Two things he here tells them further concerning the sending of the Holy Ghost:— <div eID="gen28098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28099" type="x-p"/> (1.) On whose account he should be sent: "The Father will send him <hi type="italic">in my name;</hi> that is, for <hi type="italic">my sake,</hi> at my special instance and request:" or, "as my agent and representative." He came in his Father's name, as his ambassador: the Spirit comes in his name, as resident in his absence, to carry on his undertaking, and to ripen things for his second coming. Hence he is called <hi type="italic">the Spirit of Christ,</hi> for he pleads his cause, and does his work. <div eID="gen28099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28100" type="x-p"/> (2.) On what errand he should be sent; two things he shall do:—[1.] <hi type="italic">He shall teach you all things,</hi> as a Spirit of wisdom and revelation Christ was a teacher to his disciples; if he leave them now that they have made so little proficiency, what will become of them? Why, the Spirit shall teach them, shall be their standing tutor. He shall teach them all things necessary for them either to learn themselves, or to teach others. For those that would teach the things of God must first themselves be taught of God; this is the Spirit's work. See <reference osisRef="Isa.59.21">Isa. lix. 21</reference>. [2.] <hi type="italic">He shall bring all things to your remembrance whatsoever I have said unto you.</hi> Many a good lesson Christ had taught them, which they had forgotten, and which would be to seek when they had occasion for it. Many things they did not retain the remembrance of, because they did not rightly understand the meaning of them. The Spirit shall not teach them a new gospel, but bring to their minds that which they had been taught, by leading them into the understanding of it. The apostles were all of them to preach, and some of them to write, the things that Jesus did and taught, to transmit them to distant nations and future ages; now, if they had been left to themselves herein, some needful things might have been forgotten, others misrepresented, through the treachery of their memories; therefore the Spirit is promised to enable them truly to relate and record what Christ said unto them. And to all the saints the Spirit of grace is given to be a remembrancer, and to him by faith and prayer we should commit the keeping of what we hear and know. <div eID="gen28100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28101" type="x-p"/> II. That they should be under the influence of his peace (<reference osisRef="John.14.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Peace I leave with you.</hi> When Christ was about to leave the world he <hi type="italic">made his will.</hi> His soul he committed to his Father; his body he bequeathed to Joseph, to be decently interred; his clothes fell to the soldiers; his mother he left to the care of John: but what should he leave to his poor disciples, that had left all for him? Silver and gold he had none; but he left them that which was infinitely better, <hi type="italic">his peace.</hi> <hi type="italic">"I leave you,</hi> but I leave <hi type="italic">my peace</hi> with you. I not only give you a title to it, but put you in possession of it." He did not part in anger, but in love; for this was his farewell, <hi type="italic">Peace I leave with you,</hi> as a dying father leaves portions to his children; and this is a <hi type="italic">worthy portion.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen28101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28102" type="x-p"/> 1. The legacy that is here bequeathed <hi type="italic">Peace, my peace.</hi> Peace is put for all good, and Christ has left us all needful good, all that is really and truly good, as all the purchased promised good. Peace is put for reconciliation and love; the peace bequeathed is peace with God, peace with one another; peace <hi type="italic">in our own bosoms</hi> seems to be especially meant; a tranquillity of mind arising from a sense of our justification before God. It is the counterpart of our pardons, and the composure of our minds. This Christ calls <hi type="italic">his</hi> peace, for he is himself our peace, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Eph. ii. 14</reference>. It is the peace he purchased for us and preached to us, and on which the angels congratulated men at his birth, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Luke ii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen28102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28103" type="x-p"/> 2. To whom this legacy is bequeathed: "To you, my disciples and followers, that will be exposed to trouble, and have need of peace; to you that are the sons of peace, and are qualified to receive it." This legacy was left to them as the representatives of the church, to them and their successors, to them and all true Christians in all ages. <div eID="gen28103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28104" type="x-p"/> 3. In what manner it is left: <hi type="italic">Not as the world giveth, give I unto you.</hi> That is, (1.) "I do not compliment you with <hi type="italic">Peace be unto you;</hi> no, it is not a mere formality, but a real blessing." (2.) "The peace I give is of such a nature that the smiles of the world cannot give it, nor the frowns of the world take it away." Or, (3.) "The gifts I give to you are not such as this world gives to its children and votaries, to whom it is kind." The world's gifts concern only the body and time; Christ's gifts enrich the soul for eternity: the world gives lying vanities, and that which will cheat us; Christ gives substantial blessings, which will never fail us: the world gives and takes; Christ gives a good part that shall <hi type="italic">never be taken away.</hi> (4.) The peace which Christ gives is infinitely more valuable than that which the world gives. The world's peace begins in ignorance, consists with sin, and ends in endless troubles; Christ's peace begins in grace, consists with no allowed sin, and ends at length in everlasting peace. As is the difference between a killing lethargy and a reviving refreshing sleep, such is the difference between Christ's peace and the world's. <div eID="gen28104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28105" type="x-p"/> 4. What use they should make of it: <hi type="italic">Let not your heart be troubled,</hi> for any evils past or present, <hi type="italic">neither let it be afraid</hi> of any evil to come. Note, Those that are interested in the covenant of grace, and entitled to the peace which Christ gives, ought not to yield to overwhelming griefs and fears. This comes in here as the conclusion of the whole matter; he had said (<reference osisRef="John.14.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let not your heart be troubled,</hi> and here he repeats it as that for which he had now given sufficient reason.
entries.88ee5da2de54aefcc1134f9f8b801a4ce0363234: <div eID="gen28105" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Consolatory Discourse.</title> <div sID="gen28106" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Ye have heard how I said unto you, I go away, and come <hi type="italic">again</hi> unto you. If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father: for my Father is greater than I. <hi type="super">29</hi> And now I have told you before it come to pass, that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe. <hi type="super">30</hi> Hereafter I will not talk much with you: for the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me. <hi type="super">31</hi> But that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do. Arise, let us go hence. <div eID="gen28106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28107" type="x-p"/> Christ here gives his disciples another reason why their hearts should not be troubled for his going away; and that is, because his heart was not. And here he tells them what it was that enabled him to endure the cross and despise the shame, that they might <hi type="italic">look unto him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">run with patience.</hi> He comforted himself, <div eID="gen28107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28108" type="x-p"/> I. That, though he went away, he should <hi type="italic">come again: "You have heard how I have said,</hi> and now I say it again, <hi type="italic">I go away, and come again.</hi>" Note, What we have heard of the doctrine of Christ, especially concerning his second coming, we have need to be told again and again. When we are under the power of any transport of passion, grief, or fear, or care, we forget that Christ will come again. See <reference osisRef="Phil.4.5">Phil. iv. 5</reference>. Christ encouraged himself with <hi type="italic">this,</hi> in his sufferings and death, that he should <hi type="italic">come again,</hi> and the same should comfort us in our departure at death; we go away to come again; the leave we take of our friends at that parting is only a good night, not a final farewell. See <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13-1Thess.4.14">1 Thess. iv. 13, 14</reference>. <div eID="gen28108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28109" type="x-p"/> II. That he <hi type="italic">went to his Father: "If you loved me,</hi> as by your sorrow you say you do, <hi type="italic">you would rejoice</hi> instead of mourning, because, though I leave you, yet I said, <hi type="italic">I go unto the Father,</hi> not only mine, but yours, which will be my advancement and your advantage; for <hi type="italic">my Father is greater than I.</hi>" Observe here, 1. It is matter of joy to Christ's disciples that he is gone to the Father, to take possession for orphans, and make intercession for transgressors. His departure had a bright side as well as a dark side. Therefore he sent this message after his resurrection (<reference osisRef="John.20.17">ch. xx. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">I ascend to my Father and your Father,</hi> as most comfortable. 2. The reason of this is, because <hi type="italic">the Father is greater than he,</hi> which, if it be a proper proof of that for which it is alleged (as no doubt it is), must be understood thus, that his state with his Father would be much more excellent and glorious than his present state; his returning to his Father (so Dr. Hammond) would be the advancing of him to a much higher condition than that which he was now in. Or thus, His going to the Father himself, and bringing all his followers to him there, was the ultimate end of his undertaking, and therefore greater than the means. Thus Christ raises the thoughts and expectations of his disciples to something greater than that in which now they thought all their happiness bound up. The kingdom of the Father, wherein he shall be all in all, will be greater than the mediatorial kingdom. 3. The disciples of Christ should show that they love him by their rejoicing in the glories of his exaltation, rather than by lamenting the sorrows of his humiliation, and rejoicing that he is gone to his Father, where he would be, and where we shall be shortly with him. Many that love Christ, let their love run out in a wrong channel; they think if they love him they must be continually in pain because of him; whereas those that love him should <hi type="italic">dwell at ease</hi> in him, should <hi type="italic">rejoice in Christ Jesus.</hi> <div eID="gen28109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28110" type="x-p"/> III. That his going away, compared with the prophecies which went before of it, would be a means of confirming the faith of his disciples (<reference osisRef="John.14.29">v. 29</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have told you before it come to pass</hi> that I must die and rise again, and ascend to the Father, and send the Comforter, <hi type="italic">that, when it is come to pass, you might believe.</hi>" See this reason, <reference osisRef="John.13.19">ch. xiii. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.4">xvi. 4</reference>. Christ told his disciples of his death, though he knew it would both puzzle them and grieve them, because it would afterwards redound to the confirmation of their faith in two things:—1. That he who foretold these things had a divine prescience, and knew beforehand what day would bring forth. When St. Paul was going to Jerusalem, he <hi type="italic">knew not the things that did abide him there,</hi> but Christ did. 2. That the things foretold were according to the divine purpose and designation, not sudden resolves, but the counterparts of an eternal counsel. Let them therefore not be troubled at that which would be for the confirmation of their faith, and so would redound to their real benefit; for the <hi type="italic">trial of our faith</hi> is very precious, though it cost us present <hi type="italic">heaviness, through manifold temptations,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.6">1 Pet. i. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen28110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28111" type="x-p"/> IV. That he was sure of a victory over Satan, with whom he knew he was to have a struggle in his departure (<reference osisRef="John.14.30">v. 30</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Henceforth I will not talk much with you,</hi> having not much to say, but what may be adjourned to the pouring out of the Spirit." He had a great deal of good talk with them after this (<reference osisRef="John.15.1-John.16.33">ch. xv. and xvi.</reference>), but, in comparison with what he had said, it was not much. His time was now short, and he therefore spoke largely to them now, because the opportunity would soon be over. Note, We should always endeavour to talk to the purpose, because perhaps we may not have time to talk much. We know not how soon our breath may be stopped, and therefore should be always breathing something that is good. When we come to be sick and die, perhaps we may not be capable of talking much to those about us; and therefore what good counsel we have to give them, let us give it while we are in health. One reason why he would not talk much with them was because he had now other work to apply himself to: <hi type="italic">The prince of this world comes.</hi> He called the devil the <hi type="italic">prince of this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.31">ch. xii. 31</reference>. The disciples dreamed of their Master being the prince of this world, and they worldly princes under him. But Christ tells them that the <hi type="italic">prince of this world</hi> was his enemy, and so were the <hi type="italic">princes of this world,</hi> that were actuated and ruled by him, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>. But <hi type="italic">he has nothing in me.</hi> Observe here, 1. The prospect Christ had of an approaching conflict, not only with men, but with the powers of darkness. The devil had set upon him with his temptations (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11">Matt. iv.</reference>), had offered him the <hi type="italic">kingdoms of this world,</hi> if he would hold them as tributary to him, with an eye to which Christ calls him, in disdain, <hi type="italic">the prince of this world. Then the devil departed from him for a season;</hi> "But now," says Christ, "I see him rallying again, preparing to make a furious onset, and so to gain by terrors that which he could not gain by allurements;" to frighten from his undertaking, when he could not entice from it. Note, The foresight of a temptation gives us great advantage in our resistance of it; for, being fore-warned, we should be fore-armed. While we are here, we may see Satan continually coming against us, and ought therefore to be always upon our guard. 2. The assurance he had of good success in the conflict: <hi type="italic">He hath nothing in me,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ouk echei ouden</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He hath nothing at all.</hi> (1.) There was no guilt in Christ to give authority to <hi type="italic">the prince of this world</hi> in his terrors. The devil is said to have <hi type="italic">the power of death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb. ii. 14</reference>); the Jews called him <hi type="italic">the angel of death,</hi> as an executioner. Now Christ having done no evil, Satan had no legal power against him, and therefore, though he prevailed to crucify him, he could not prevail to terrify him; though he hurried him to death, yet not to despair. When Satan comes to disquiet us, he has something in us to perplex us with, for we have all sinned; but, when he would disturb Christ, he found no occasion against him. (2.) There was no corruption in Christ, to give advantage to <hi type="italic">the prince of this world</hi> in his temptations. He could not crush his undertaking by drawing him to sin, because there was nothing sinful in him, nothing irregular for his temptations to fasten upon, no tinder for him to strike fire into; such was the spotless purity of his nature that he was above the possibility of sinning. The more Satan's interest in us is crushed and decays, the more comfortably may we expect sufferings and death. <div eID="gen28111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28112" type="x-p"/> V. That his departure was in compliance with, and obedience to, his Father. Satan could not force his life from him, and yet he would die: <hi type="italic">that the world may know that I love the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.31">v. 31</reference>. We may take this, <div eID="gen28112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28113" type="x-p"/> 1. As confirming what he had often said, that his undertaking, as Mediator, was a demonstration to the world, (1.) Of his compliance with the Father; hereby it appeared that he loved the Father. As it was an evidence of his love to man that he died for his salvation, so it was of his love to God that he died for his glory and the accomplishing of his purposes. Let the world know that between the Father and the Son there is not love lost. <hi type="italic">As the Father loved the Son, and gave all things into his hands;</hi> so <hi type="italic">the Son loved the Father,</hi> and <hi type="italic">gave his spirit into his hand.</hi> (2.) Of his obedience to his Father: "<hi type="italic">As the Father gave me commandment, even so I</hi> did—did the thing commanded me in the manner commanded." Note, The best evidence of our love to the Father is our doing as he hath given us commandment. As Christ loved the Father, and obeyed him, <hi type="italic">even to the death,</hi> so we must love Christ, and obey him. Christ's eye to the Father's commandment, obliging him to suffer and die, bore him up with cheerfulness, and overcame the reluctancies of nature; this took off the offence of the cross, that what he did was by order from the Father. The command of God is sufficient to bear us out in that which is most disputed by others, and therefore should be sufficient to bear us up in that which is most difficult to ourselves: <hi type="italic">This is the will of him</hi> that made me, <hi type="italic">that sent me.</hi> <div eID="gen28113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28114" type="x-p"/> 2. As concluding what he had now said; having brought it to this, here he leaves it: <hi type="italic">that the world may know that I love the Father.</hi> You shall see how cheerfully I can meet the appointed cross: "<hi type="italic">Arise, let us go hence</hi> to the garden;" so some; or, to <hi type="italic">Jerusalem.</hi> When we talk of troubles at a distance, it is easy to say, <hi type="italic">Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest;</hi> but when it comes to the pinch, when an unavoidable cross lies in the way of duty, then to say, "<hi type="italic">Arise, let us go</hi> to meet it," instead of going out of our way to miss it, this lets <hi type="italic">the world know that we love the Father.</hi> If this discourse was at the close of the passover-supper, it should seem that at these words he arose from the table, and retired into the drawing-room, where he might the more freely carry on the discourse with his disciples in the following chapters, and pray with them. Dr. Goodwin's remark upon this is, that Christ mentioning the great motive of his sufferings, his Father's commandment, was in all haste to go forth to suffer and die, was afraid of slipping the time of Judas's meeting him: <hi type="italic">Arise,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">let us go hence</hi> but he looks upon the glass, as it were, sees it not quite out, and therefore sits down again, and preaches another sermon. Now, (1.) In these words he gives his disciples an encouragement to follow him. He does not say, <hi type="italic">I must go;</hi> but, <hi type="italic">Let us go.</hi> He calls them out to no hardships but what he himself goes before them in as their leader. They had promised they would not desert him: "Come," says he, "<hi type="italic">let us go</hi> then; let us see how you will make the words good." (2.) He gives them an example, teaching them at all times, especially in suffering times, to sit loose to all things here below, and often to think and speak of leaving them. Though we sit easy, and in the midst of the delights of an agreeable conversation, yet we must not think of being here always: <hi type="italic">Arise, let us go hence.</hi> If it was at the close of the paschal and eucharistical supper, it teaches us that the solemnities of our communion with God are not to be constant in this world. When we sit down under Christ's shadow with delight, and say, <hi type="italic">It is good to be here;</hi> yet we must think of rising and going hence; going down from the mount.  <chapter eID="John.14"/> <div eID="gen28114" type="x-p"/>

entries.296c6f19d3adc748fcce7e6d1ad7d8f588ea4cff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15317"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.14.1-John.14.31">Joh 14:1-31</reference>. Discourse at the Table, after Supper.</title> <div sID="gen29459" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We now come to that portion of the evangelical history which we may with propriety call its Holy of Holies. Our Evangelist, like a consecrated priest, alone opens up to us the view into this sanctuary. It is the record of the last moments spent by the Lord in the midst of His disciples before His passion, when words full of heavenly thought flowed from His sacred lips. All that His heart, glowing with love, had still to say to His friends, was compressed into this short season. At first (from <reference osisRef="John.13.31">Joh 13:31</reference>) the intercourse took the form of conversation; sitting at table, they talked familiarly together. But when (<reference osisRef="John.14.31">Joh 14:31</reference>) the repast was finished, the language of Christ assumed a loftier strain; the disciples, assembled around their Master, listened to the words of life, and seldom spoke a word (only <reference osisRef="John.16.17">Joh 16:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.16.29">29</reference>). "At length, in the Redeemer's sublime intercessory prayer, His full soul was poured forth in express petitions to His heavenly Father on behalf of those who were His own. It is a peculiarity of these last chapters, that they treat almost exclusively of the most profound relations--</hi>as that of the Son to the Father, and of both to the Spirit, that of Christ to the Church, of the Church to the world, and so forth. Moreover, a considerable portion of these sublime communications surpassed the point of view to which the disciples had at that time attained; hence the Redeemer frequently repeats the same sentiments in order to impress them more deeply upon their minds, and, because of what they still did not understand, points them to the Holy Spirit, who would remind them of all His sayings, and lead them into all truth (<reference osisRef="John.14.26">Joh 14:26</reference>)" [Olshausen].<div eID="gen29459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29460" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15317"/><hi type="bold">1. Let not your heart be troubled, &c.--</hi>What myriads of souls have not these opening words cheered, in deepest gloom, since first they were uttered!<div eID="gen29460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29461" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye believe in God--</hi>absolutely.<div eID="gen29461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believe also in me--</hi>that is, Have the same trust in Me. What less, and what else, can these words mean? And if so, what a demand to make by one sitting familiarly with them at the supper table! Compare the saying in <reference osisRef="John.5.17">Joh 5:17</reference>, for which the Jews took up stones to stone Him, as "making himself equal with God" (<reference osisRef="John.14.18">Joh 14:18</reference>). But it is no transfer of our trust from its proper Object; it is but the concentration of our trust in the Unseen and Impalpable One upon His Own Incarnate Son, by which that trust, instead of the distant, unsteady, and too often cold and scarce real thing it otherwise is, acquires a conscious reality, warmth, and power, which makes all things new. This is Christianity in brief. <div eID="gen29462" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c1b7da0eb9a84729df7d4c7ac497a05a15b01f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15318"/><div sID="gen29463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15318"/><hi type="bold">2. In my Father's house are many mansions--</hi>and so room for all, and a place for each.<div eID="gen29463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if not, I would have told you--</hi>that is, I would tell you so at once; I would not deceive you.<div eID="gen29464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I go to prepare a place for you--</hi>to obtain for you a right to be there, and to possess your "place." <div eID="gen29465" type="x-p"/>
entries.73334044bdbfedeaa69fd0a1d665d8f2d5c9d602: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15319"/><div sID="gen29466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15319"/><hi type="bold">3. I will come again and receive you unto myself--</hi>strictly, at His Personal appearing; but in a secondary and comforting sense, to each individually. Mark again the claim made:--to come again to receive His people to Himself, that where He is there they may be also. He thinks it ought to be enough to be assured that they shall be where He is and in His keeping. <div eID="gen29466" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb0126bea958e1715f8fc5a0f0061bf7b5e79e99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15320"/><div sID="gen29467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15320"/><hi type="bold">4-7. whither I go ye know ... Thomas saith, Lord, we know not whither thou guest ... Jesus saith, I am the way, &c.--</hi>By saying this, He meant rather to draw out their inquiries and reply to them. Christ is "THE Way" to the Father--"no man cometh unto the Father but by Me"; He is "THE Truth" of all we find in the Father when we get to Him, "For in Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.9">Col 2:9</reference>), and He is all "THE Life" that shall ever flow to us and bless us from the Godhead thus approached and thus manifested in Him--"this is the true God and eternal life" (<reference osisRef="1John.5.20">1Jo 5:20</reference>). <div eID="gen29467" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f98b5b87c23a61dffe6bef9240e1ca06f2ae19f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15322"/><div sID="gen29469" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15322"/><hi type="bold">8-12. The substance of this passage is that the Son is the ordained and perfect manifestation of the Father, that His own word for this ought to His disciples to be enough; that if any doubts remained His works ought to remove them (see on <reference osisRef="John.10.37">Joh 10:37</reference>); but yet that these works of His were designed merely to aid weak faith, and would be repeated, nay exceeded, by His disciples, in virtue of the power He would confer on them after His departure. His miracles the apostles wrought, though wholly in His name and by His power, and the "greater" works--</hi>not in degree but in kind--were the conversion of thousands in a day, by His Spirit accompanying them. <div eID="gen29469" type="x-p"/>
entries.35c10a3a39c83affec94c01643b932b93cbdff70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15323"/><div sID="gen29470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15323"/><hi type="bold">13-14. whatsoever ye ... ask in my name--</hi>as Mediator.<div eID="gen29470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that will I do--</hi>as Head and Lord of the kingdom of God. This comprehensive promise is emphatically repeated in <reference osisRef="John.14.14">Joh 14:14</reference>. <div eID="gen29471" type="x-p"/>
entries.90b210f06c874fe7bd78cd7e6da372a9cfad4883: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15324"/><div sID="gen29472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15324"/><hi type="bold">15-17. If ye love me, keep my commandments. And I will pray the Father, &c.--</hi>This connection seems designed to teach that the proper temple for the indwelling Spirit of Jesus is a heart filled with that love to Him which lives actively for Him, and so this was the fitting preparation for the promised gift.<div eID="gen29472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall give you another Comforter--</hi>a word used only by John; in his Gospel with reference to the Holy Spirit, in his First Epistle (<reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1Jo 2:1</reference>), with reference to Christ Himself. Its proper sense is an "advocate," "patron," "helper." In this sense it is plainly meant of Christ (<reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1Jo 2:1</reference>), and in this sense it comprehends all the comfort as well as aid of the Spirit's work. The Spirit is here promised as One who would supply Christ's own place in His absence.<div eID="gen29473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he may abide with you for ever--</hi>never go away, as Jesus was going to do in the body. <div eID="gen29474" type="x-p"/>
entries.623f470e9f7ecaccd6c7c109c5e57efdda5e0f0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15326"/><div sID="gen29477" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15326"/><hi type="bold">18-20. I will not leave you comfortless--</hi>in a bereaved and desolate condition; or (as in Margin) "orphans."<div eID="gen29477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will come to you--</hi>"I come" or "am coming" to you; that is, plainly by the Spirit, since it was to make His departure to be no bereavement. <div eID="gen29478" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6136e9f331c4f063113b821a8083d6658a53492: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15329"/><div sID="gen29485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15329"/><hi type="bold">21. He that hath my commandments and keepeth them, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.14.15">Joh 14:15</reference>).<div eID="gen29485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my Father and I will love him--</hi>Mark the sharp line of distinction here, not only between the Divine Persons but the actings of love in Each respectively, towards true disciples. <div eID="gen29486" type="x-p"/>
entries.08bdbf8cba0ec90d93ed2d898f021a655418410c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15330"/><div sID="gen29487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15330"/><hi type="bold">22. Judas saith ... not Iscariot--</hi>Beautiful parenthesis this! The traitor being no longer present, we needed not to be told that this question came not from him. But it is as if the Evangelist had said, "A very different Judas from the traitor, and a very different question from any that he would have put. Indeed [as one in Stier says], we never read of Iscariot that he entered in any way into his Master's words, or ever put a question even of rash curiosity (though it may be he did, but that nothing from him was deemed fit for immortality in the Gospels but his name and treason)."<div eID="gen29487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how ... manifest thyself to us, and not to the world--</hi>a most natural and proper question, founded on <reference osisRef="John.14.19">Joh 14:19</reference>, though interpreters speak against it as Jewish. <div eID="gen29488" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3d80bd908dba639626fd5b99a459a22bc0e8498: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15331"/><div sID="gen29489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15331"/><hi type="bold">23. we will come and make our abode with him--</hi>Astonishing statement! In the Father's "coming" He "refers to the revelation of Him as a Father to the soul, which does not take place till the Spirit comes into the heart, teaching it to cry, Abba, Father" [Olshausen]. The "abode" means a permanent, eternal stay! (Compare <reference osisRef="Lev.26.11">Le 26:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.26">Eze 37:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.16">2Co 6:16</reference>; and contrast <reference osisRef="Jer.14.8">Jr 14:8</reference>). <div eID="gen29489" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4f0075e3f6aab198d8034ee2075cd58b656884c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15332"/><div sID="gen29490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15332"/><hi type="bold">25-26. he shall teach you all things, and bring all to ... remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.14.15">Joh 14:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.17">Joh 14:17</reference>). As the Son came in the Father's name, so the Father shall send the Spirit in My name, says Jesus, that is, with like divine power and authority to reproduce in their souls what Christ taught them, "bringing to living consciousness what lay like slumbering germs in their minds" [Olshausen]. On this rests the credibility and ultimate divine authority of THE Gospel history. The whole of what is here said of THE Spirit is decisive of His divine personality. "He who can regard all the personal expressions, applied to the Spirit in these three chapters ('teaching,' 'reminding,' 'testifying,' 'coming,' 'convincing,' 'guiding,' 'speaking,' 'hearing,' 'prophesying,' 'taking') as being no other than a long drawn-out figure, deserves not to be recognized even as an interpreter of intelligible words, much less an expositor of Holy Scripture" [Stier]. <div eID="gen29490" type="x-p"/>
entries.e536ae0ab5d0ab5a43e591a067fcc352fd3986cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15333"/><div sID="gen29491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15333"/><hi type="bold">27. Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you--</hi>If <reference osisRef="John.14.25">Joh 14:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.26">26</reference> sounded like a note of preparation for drawing the discourse to a close, this would sound like a farewell. But oh, how different from ordinary adieus! It is a parting word, but of richest import, the customary "peace" of a parting friend sublimed and transfigured. As "the Prince of Peace" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>) He brought it into flesh, carried it about in His Own Person ("My peace") died to make it ours, left it as the heritage of His disciples upon earth, implants and maintains it by His Spirit in their hearts. Many a legacy is "left" that is never "given" to the legatee, many a gift destined that never reaches its proper object. But Christ is the Executor of His own Testament; the peace He "leaves" He "gives"; Thus all is secure.<div eID="gen29491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not as the world giveth--</hi>in contrast with the world, He gives sincerely, substantially, eternally. <div eID="gen29492" type="x-p"/>
entries.653ce48e637ecf8690734c1c506f31ef7126c325: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15334"/><div sID="gen29493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15334"/><hi type="bold">28. If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father, for my Father is greater than I--</hi>These words, which Arians and Socinians perpetually quote as triumphant evidence against the proper Divinity of Christ, really yield no intelligible sense on their principles. Were a holy man on his deathbed, beholding his friends in tears at the prospect of losing him, to say, "Ye ought rather to joy than weep for me, and would if ye really loved me, "the speech would be quite natural. But if they should ask him, why joy at his departure was more suitable than sorrow, would they not start back with astonishment, if not horror, were he to reply, "Because my Father is greater than I?" Does not this strange speech from Christ's lips, then, presuppose such teaching on His part as would make it extremely difficult for them to think He could gain anything by departing to the Father, and make it necessary for Him to say expressly that there was a sense in which He could do so? Thus, this startling explanation seems plainly intended to correct such misapprehensions as might arise from the emphatic and reiterated teaching of His proper equality with the Father--as if so Exalted a Person were incapable of any accession by transition from this dismal scene to a cloudless heaven and the very bosom of the Father--and by assuring them that this was not the case, to make them forget their own sorrow in His approaching joy. <div eID="gen29493" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc90903cf34b636ec49077dd07a21c9c93ab0b4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15335"/><div sID="gen29494" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15335"/><hi type="bold">30-31. Hereafter I will not talk much with you--</hi>"I have a little more to say, but My work hastens apace, and the approach of the adversary will cut it short."<div eID="gen29494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the prince of this world--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>).<div eID="gen29495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cometh--</hi>with hostile intent, for a last grand attack, having failed in His first formidable assault (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.1-Luke.4.13">Lu 4:1-13</reference>) from which he "departed [only] for a season" (<reference osisRef="John.14.13">Joh 14:13</reference>).<div eID="gen29496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and hath nothing in me--</hi>nothing of His own--nothing to fasten on. Glorious saying! The truth of it is, that which makes the Person and Work of Christ the life of the world (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">He 9:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.5">1Jo 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>). <div eID="gen29497" type="x-p"/>

entries.d81a8f4d43c015172275c543d9416ee791f36403: <div eID="gen42581" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen42582" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen42583" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen42583" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen42582" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen42584" type="x-p"/> Christ comforts his disciples, on the event of his removal from them, by the consideration of his going to prepare a place for them in heaven, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.1-Joh.14.4">Joh 14:1-4</reference>. Thomas questions him concerning the way to the Father, and is answered, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.5-Joh.14.7">Joh 14:5-7</reference>. Philip proposes a difficulty, and Christ shows that he and the Father are one; that he is Mediator between God and man; and that whatsoever is asked in his name shall be obtained, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.8-Joh.14.14">Joh 14:8-14</reference>. He promises them the Holy Spirit as the Comforter and Spirit of truth, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.15-Joh.14.18">Joh 14:15-18</reference>. Shows them that he is shortly to leave them, and that those who love him should be loved of the Father, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.19-Joh.14.21">Joh 14:19-21</reference>. Jude asks a question, how Christ is to manifest himself to the disciples, and not to the Jews? <reference osisRef="Joh.14.22">Joh 14:22</reference>. Christ answers, and shows that the manifestation is to be made to those who love God, and to them the Holy Spirit is to be an infallible teacher, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.23-Joh.14.26">Joh 14:23-26</reference>. He bequeaths his peace to them, and fortifies them against discouragements, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.27-Joh.14.29">Joh 14:27-29</reference>. Foretells his approaching death, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.30">Joh 14:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.31">Joh 14:31</reference>. <div eID="gen42584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42585" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen42585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42586" type="x-p"/> Let not your heart be troubled - After having answered St. Peter's question, he addresses himself again to his disciples, and tells them not to be afflicted at his leaving them, nor to lose courage because of what he said concerning Peter's denying him; that if they reposed their confidence in God, he would protect them; and that, howsoever they might see him treated, they should believe in him more firmly, as his sufferings, death, and resurrection should be to them the most positive proof of his being the Messiah, the Savior of the world. <div eID="gen42586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42587" type="x-p"/> Ye believe in God, believe also in me - It is best to read both the verbs in the imperative mood: - Place your confidence in God, and in me as the Mediator between God and man, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.12-Joh.14.14">Joh 14:12-14</reference>; and expect the utmost support from God; but expect it all through me. The disciples began to lose all hope of a secular kingdom, and were discouraged in consequence: Christ promises them a spiritual and heavenly inheritance, and thus lifts up their drooping hearts.
entries.4c30a21073da6893cd375f1282a9149fb80d5d0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen42587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42588" type="x-p"/> In my Father's house, etc. - The kingdom of glory. <div eID="gen42588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42589" type="x-p"/> Many mansions - Though I have said before that whither I am going ye cannot come now, yet do not think that we shall be for ever separated. I am going to that state of glory where there is not only a place of supreme eminence for myself, but also places for all my disciples; - various degrees of glory, suited to the various capacities and attainments of my followers. <div eID="gen42589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42590" type="x-p"/> Our Lord alludes here to the temple, which was called the house of God, in the precincts of which there were a great number of chambers, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.5">1Kgs 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezr.8.29">Ezr 8:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.35.2">Jer 35:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.35.4">Jer 35:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.10">Jer 36:10</reference>. <div eID="gen42590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42591" type="x-p"/> If - not - I would have told you - If your places were not prepared in the kingdom of God, I would not have permitted you to have indulged a vain hope concerning future blessedness.
entries.6c8fc8fb66d092072b814aedb2112cce8c239dcc: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen42591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42592" type="x-p"/> And if I go - And when I shall have gone and prepared a place for you - opened the kingdom of an eternal glory for your reception, and for the reception of all that shall die in the faith, I will come again, after my resurrection, and give you the fullest assurances of this state of blessedness; and confirm you in the faith, by my grace and the effusion of my Spirit. Dr. Lightfoot thinks, and with great probability too, that there is an allusion here to <reference osisRef="Num.10.33">Num 10:33</reference> : And the ark of the Lord went before them to search out a resting place for them.
entries.9617c3738ff78288d3e19de4b266e4fa92d7980a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen42592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42593" type="x-p"/> And whither I go ye know - I have told you this so often and so plainly that ye must certainly have comprehended what I have said.
entries.afc45dde0a95fd4df506ef097e7c0f37b7a5eac5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen42593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42594" type="x-p"/> Lord, we know not - Thomas, perhaps, thought that our Lord only spoke of his going some distance from the place where he then was.
entries.f84b013f30d5ec69f5ec422532746f39d9b970b6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen42594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42595" type="x-p"/> I am the Way - That leads so the Father: - the Truth that teaches the knowledge of God, and directs in the way: - the Life that animates all those who seek and serve him, and which is to be enjoyed eternally at the end of the way. <div eID="gen42595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42596" type="x-p"/> Christ is the Way: <div eID="gen42596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42597" type="x-p"/> 1. By his doctrine, <reference osisRef="Joh.6.68">Joh 6:68</reference>. <div eID="gen42597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42598" type="x-p"/> 2. By his example, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.21">1Pet 2:21</reference>. <div eID="gen42598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42599" type="x-p"/> 3. By his sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.8">Heb 9:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.9">Heb 9:9</reference>. <div eID="gen42599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42600" type="x-p"/> 4. By his Spirit, <reference osisRef="Joh.16.13">Joh 16:13</reference>. <div eID="gen42600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42601" type="x-p"/> He is the Truth: <div eID="gen42601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42602" type="x-p"/> 1. In opposition to all false religions. <div eID="gen42602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42603" type="x-p"/> 2. To the Mosaic law, which was only the shadow, not the truth or substance, of the good things which were to come. And <div eID="gen42603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42604" type="x-p"/> 3. In respect to all the promises of God, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">2Cor 1:20</reference>. <div eID="gen42604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42605" type="x-p"/> He is the Life, both in grace and glory; the life that not only saves from death, but destroys it. <div eID="gen42605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42606" type="x-p"/> No man cometh unto the Father - By any other doctrine, by any other merit, or by any other intercession than mine.
entries.e6ce1a984ca438580c33da8585df91a74dbd19a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen42606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42607" type="x-p"/> If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father - Because I and the Father are One, <reference osisRef="Joh.10.30">Joh 10:30</reference>. Or, if ye had properly examined the intention and design of the law, ye would have been convinced that it referred to me; and that all that I have done and instituted was according to the design and intention of the Father, as expressed in that law.
entries.2fab9f983cf45ef2de2ede32bd90184848fbeae4: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen42607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42608" type="x-p"/> Show us the Father - As if he had said, We have seen and adored thee, and our happiness will be complete if thou show us the Father. The demand of Philip was similar to that made by Moses, <reference osisRef="Exo.33.18">Exo 33:18</reference>. He wished to see the glory of God. In Peter, James, or John, this would have been inexcusable; but Philip had not seen the transfiguration on the mount. The Jewish history is full of the manifestations which God made of himself, and especially when he gave the law. As Christ was introducing a new law, Philip wished to have an additional manifestation of God.
entries.232ff5418c22cab70872605ad54fd9c3ffaa9c0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen42608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42609" type="x-p"/> He that hath seen me hath seen the Father - Could any creature say these words? Do they not evidently imply that Christ declared himself to his disciples to be the everlasting God?
entries.9c4a75dc8d24f808de70cc13cb91aef70c40d9e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen42609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42610" type="x-p"/> I am in the Father, and the Father in me? - We are essentially one; and those who have seen me have seen him who sent me. <div eID="gen42610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42611" type="x-p"/> He doeth the works - We are not only one in nature, but one also in operation. The works which I have done bear witness of the infinite perfection of my nature. Such miracles as I have wrought could only be performed by unlimited power.
entries.4d4e9a37b7f0844b4a197fe6e4f581880ee2da54: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen42611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42612" type="x-p"/> And greater works than these - The miracles which I have wrought could not have been wrought but by the omnipotence of God; but that omnipotence can work greater. And those who believe on my name shall, through my almighty power, be enabled to work greater miracles than those which l have ordinarily wrought. An impostor might seduce the people by false miracles; but he could not make his power and cunning pass to all those who were seduced by him: but I will give you this proof of the divinity of my mission and the truth of my doctrine. <div eID="gen42612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42613" type="x-p"/> Perhaps the greater works refer to the immense multitudes that were brought to God by the ministry of the apostles. By the apostles was the doctrine of Christ spread far and wide; while Christ confined his ministry chiefly to the precincts of Judea. It is certainly the greatest miracle of Divine grace to convert the obstinate, wicked heart of man from sin to holiness. This was done in numberless cases by the disciples, who were endued with power from on high, while proclaiming remission of sins through faith in his blood. <div eID="gen42613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42614" type="x-p"/> Some account for the greater works thus: <div eID="gen42614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42615" type="x-p"/> 1. The very shadow of Peter healed the diseased, <reference osisRef="Act.5.15">Act 5:15</reference>. <div eID="gen42615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42616" type="x-p"/> 2. Diseases were cured, and demons cast out, by applying to the persons handkerchiefs and aprons that had before touched the body of Paul, <reference osisRef="Act.19.12">Act 19:12</reference>. <div eID="gen42616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42617" type="x-p"/> 3. By the word of Peter, Ananias and Sapphira were struck dead, <reference osisRef="Act.5.5">Act 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.5.9">Act 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.5.10">Act 5:10</reference>. <div eID="gen42617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42618" type="x-p"/> 4. Elymas the sorcerer was struck blind by the word of Paul, <reference osisRef="Act.13.11">Act 13:11</reference>. <div eID="gen42618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42619" type="x-p"/> 5. Christ only preached in Judea, and in the language only of that country; but the apostles preached through the most of the then known world, and in all the languages of all countries. But let it be remarked that all this was done by the power of Christ; and I think it still more natural to attribute the greater works to the greater number of conversions made under the apostles' ministry. The reason which our Lord gives for this is worthy of deep attention: - <div eID="gen42619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42620" type="x-p"/> Because I go unto my Father - Where I shall be an Intercessor for you, that: -
entries.bd2ebd33cd78cd8f5f58281d964a1e2b562bd227: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen42620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42621" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever ye shall ask in my name - To enable you to perform these miracles, and to convert souls, may be granted you. Besides, by going unto the Father, I shall receive the Holy Spirit, and send down his abundant influences into the hearts of those who believe.
entries.75be6d2ac5783c4472b19b21bae80471a55efbb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen42621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42622" type="x-p"/> If ye love me, keep my commandments - Do not be afflicted at the thought of my being separated from you: the most solid proof ye can give of your attachment to and affection for me is to keep my commandments. This I shall receive as a greater proof of your affection than your tears.
entries.faad035fdf9bc7ff3e0a4a92d888c40d1c9e8f20: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen42622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42623" type="x-p"/> I will pray the Father - After having made an atonement for the sin of the world, I will become the Mediator between God and man; and through my mediation and intercession shall all the blessings of grace and glory be acquired. <div eID="gen42623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42624" type="x-p"/> Another Comforter - The word παρακλητος signifies not only a comforter, but also an advocate, a defender of a cause, a counsellor, patron, mediator. Christ is thus termed, <reference osisRef="1Jn.2.1">1Jn 2:1</reference>, where the common translation renders the word advocate. Christ is thus called, because he is represented as transacting the concerns of our souls with God; and for this cause, he tells us, he goes unto the Father, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.12">Joh 14:12</reference>. The Holy Spirit is thus called, because he transacts the cause of God and Christ with us, explains to us the nature and importance of the great atonement, shows the necessity of it, counsels us to receive it, instructs us how to lay hold on it, vindicates our claim to it, and makes intercessions in us with unutterable groanings. As Christ acted with his disciples while he sojourned with them, so the Holy Ghost acts with those who believe in his name. <div eID="gen42624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42625" type="x-p"/> For ever - As the death and atonement of Christ will be necessary to man till the conclusion of the world, so the office of the Holy Spirit must be continued among men till the end of time: therefore says Christ, he shall continue with you for ever, teaching, comforting, advising, defending, and interceding for you and for all my followers to the end of time.
entries.ac10384db6f8b80f5f587a4075723fb6e35768b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen42625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42626" type="x-p"/> The Spirit of truth - The Spirit, or Holy Ghost, whose essential office is to manifest, vindicate, and apply the truth. The Gospel of Christ may be thus called, because it exposes falsity, removes error, and teaches the knowledge of the true God - shows the way to him, saves from vanity and illusive hopes, and establishes solid happiness in the souls of those who believe. <div eID="gen42626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42627" type="x-p"/> The world cannot receive - By the world, St. John means those who are influenced only by the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye, and the pride of life, <reference osisRef="1Jn.2.16">1Jn 2:16</reference>. Now these cannot receive the Spirit of the truth, because they see him not, have no spiritual discernment, attend to nothing but the dictates of their corrupt passions and affections, and will admit of no influence but what can be an object of their senses. Hence all the deign and irreligion in the world. God, in the operation of his hands, and in the influences of his Spirit, is found every where except in the perverted passions of men. In these alone do men of corrupt minds seek him; here only he is not to be found, and therefore they become infidels and atheists. <div eID="gen42627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42628" type="x-p"/> But ye know him - Ye have already received a measure of the truth, and ye believe in this Spirit. Probably our Lord refers to the knowledge which they should afterwards attain: in this sense the passage has been understood by the Vulgate, Nonnus, and two copies of the Itala, which read, Ye Shall know him. <div eID="gen42628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42629" type="x-p"/> For he dwelleth with you - Or, as the Ethiopic, Vulgate, Nonnus, and six copies of the Itala read, he shall dwell with you, (see above); and this, it is very evident, is the meaning of the evangelist, who not unfrequently uses the present for the future tense. It is certain the Holy Spirit was not yet given to the disciples so as to dwell in them; this St. John himself assures us, <reference osisRef="Joh.7.39">Joh 7:39</reference>. And it is evidently of that Spirit and its influences, which was not given till the day of pentecost, that our Lord here speaks.
entries.823319644b0c797a21b9d7880f1283c101fe50a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen42629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42630" type="x-p"/> I will not leave you comfortless - Literally, orphans. The original word ορφανος, is by some derived from ορφνος, obscure, dark, because, says Mintert, an orphan (one deprived of father and mother) is little esteemed, neglected, and is obliged to wander about in obscurity and darkness. Others derive it from the Hebrew חרף charaph, to strip or make bare, despoil, because such a child is destitute of comfort, direction, and support, and is a prey to misery and disease, to sin and to death. <div eID="gen42630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42631" type="x-p"/> The disciples of a particular teacher among the Hebrews called him father; his scholars were called his children, and, on his death, were considered as orphans. Christ calls his disciples children, beloved children, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.33">Joh 13:33</reference>; and, now that he is about to be removed from them by death, he assures them that they shall not be left fatherless, or without a teacher; for in a little time he should come again, (rise from the dead), and, after his ascension, they should be made partakers of that Spirit which would be their comforter, advocate, teacher, and guide for ever.
entries.d35aa0d296dd80e536cf558e217b0323096a28ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen42631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42632" type="x-p"/> Because I live - As surely as I shall rise from the dead, so shall ye. My resurrection shall be the proof and pledge of yours. And because I live a life of intercession for you at the right hand of God, ye shall live a life of grace and peace here, and a life of glory hereafter.
entries.e04bf22857ba2980e3ffa918837c058eb7afa7fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen42632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42633" type="x-p"/> That I am in my Father - After my resurrection, ye shall be more fully convinced of this important truth, that I and the Father are One; for I will live in you by the energy of my Spirit, and ye shall live in me by faith, love, and obedience.
entries.1bceb9b3d6b2cf31928bd9321fa1dd0eb78d59c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen42633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42634" type="x-p"/> He it is that loveth me - See on <reference osisRef="Joh.14.15">Joh 14:15</reference> (note). <div eID="gen42634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42635" type="x-p"/> And will manifest myself to him - All my faithful disciples shall see me after my resurrection; and I will manifest my power and goodness to all those who believe in and obey me, even to the end of the world.
entries.51eca376ebe6d1bd6d51a70795f8fee876701649: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen42635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42636" type="x-p"/> Judas - The same as Thaddeus and Lebbeus, the brother of James, and author of what is called the epistle of Jude. <div eID="gen42636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42637" type="x-p"/> How is it - Or, how can it be - τι γεγονεν, what is to happen? - on what account is it? Judas, who was probably thinking that the kingdom of Christ should extend over all the earth, wonders how this can be, and yet Christ manifest himself only to his disciples and not to the world, <reference osisRef="Joh.14.19">Joh 14:19</reference>. To this our Lord, in a more express manner than he had done before answers: -
entries.bd25069d2d27fcaaa07793704677bf0a5235874e: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen42637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42638" type="x-p"/> If a man - Not only my present disciples, but all those who shall believe on me through their word, or that of their successors: <div eID="gen42638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42639" type="x-p"/> Love me - Receive me as his Savior, and get the love of God shed abroad in his heart by the Holy Ghost: <div eID="gen42639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42640" type="x-p"/> He will keep my words - Observe all my sayings, and have his affections and conduct regulated by my Spirit and doctrine: <div eID="gen42640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42641" type="x-p"/> My Father will love him - Call him his child; support, defend, and preserve him as such. <div eID="gen42641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42642" type="x-p"/> And we will come unto him - God the Father, through his Son, will continue to pour out his choicest blessings upon his head and upon his heart: <div eID="gen42642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42643" type="x-p"/> And make our abode with him - Will make his heart our temple, where God, the Father, Son, and Spirit, shall rest, receive homage, and dwell to eternity. Thus will I manifest myself to the believing, loving, obedient disciple, and not to the world, who will not receive the Spirit of the truth.
entries.f9ee91f08eac9bc4b256ced1f228df82da3d30a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen42643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42644" type="x-p"/> He that loveth me not, etc. - Hence we learn that the man who is not obedient to the testimonies of Christ does not love him; and the Spirit of this truth has said, He who loves not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.22">1Cor 16:22</reference>.
entries.1e77564c999b3c5807e63bd4eec658b5c409f130: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen42644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42645" type="x-p"/> He shall teach you all things - If in the things which I have already spoken to you, there appear to you any obscurity, the Holy Spirit, the Advocate, Counsellor, and Instructer, will take away all your doubts, free you from all embarrassment, and give you a perfect understanding in all things: and this Spirit ye shall shortly receive. <div eID="gen42645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42646" type="x-p"/> And bring all things to your remembrance - Here Christ promises them that inspiration of the Holy Spirit which enabled them not only to give a true history of his life and death, but also gave them the most perfect recollection of all the words which he had spoken to them, so that they have been able to transmit to posterity the identical words which Jesus uttered in his sermons, and in his different discourses with them, the Jews, and others.
entries.2a5e3c11eab1da856f9c7fed2764b6372b1d9091: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen42646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42647" type="x-p"/> Peace I leave with you - The Jewish form of salutation and benediction. A wish of peace among them is thus to be understood: May you prosper in body and soul, and enjoy every earthly and heavenly good! For the meaning of this word, see <reference osisRef="Mat.5.9">Mat 5:9</reference>. <div eID="gen42647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42648" type="x-p"/> My peace I give unto you - Such tranquillity of soul, such uninterrupted happiness of mind, such everlasting friendship with God as I enjoy, may ye all enjoy! And such blessedness I bequeath unto you: it is my last, my best, my dying legacy. <div eID="gen42648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42649" type="x-p"/> Not as the world giveth - Not as the Jews, in empty wishes: not as the people of the world, in empty compliments. Their salutations and benedictions are generally matters of custom and polite ceremony, given without desire or design; but I mean what I say; what I wish you, that I will give you. To his followers Jesus gives peace, procures it, preserves it, and establishes it. He is the author, prince, promoter, and keeper of peace. <div eID="gen42649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42650" type="x-p"/> Neither let it be afraid - Μηδε δειλιατω, Let not your heart shrink back through fear of any approaching evil. This is the proper meaning of the word. In a few hours ye will be most powerfully assaulted; but stand firm: - the evil will only fall upon me; and this evil will result in your comfort and salvation, and in the redemption of a lost world.
entries.09384ae35715963270d457d46af1b12011fc0850: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen42650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42651" type="x-p"/> I go away - To the Father by my death: <div eID="gen42651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42652" type="x-p"/> And come again unto you - By my resurrection. <div eID="gen42652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42653" type="x-p"/> Ye would rejoice - Because, as the Messiah, I am going to receive a kingdom, and power, and glory, for ever. Therefore as my friends ye should rejoice in my elevation, though for a while it may put you to the pain of being separated from me: besides, I am going that I may send you the Holy Spirit, which shall fill you with the fullness of God: on your own account, therefore, ye should have rejoiced and not mourned. <div eID="gen42653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42654" type="x-p"/> My Father is greater than I - In <reference osisRef="Joh.14.24">Joh 14:24</reference>, Christ tells his disciples that the Father had sent him: i.e. in his quality of Messiah, he was sent by the Father to instruct, and to save mankind. Now, as the sender is greater than the sent, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.16">Joh 13:16</reference>, so in this sense is the Father greater than the Son; and in this sense was the passage understood by Origen, Jerome, Novatian, and Vigilius, who read the text thus: The Father, ὁ πεμψας, who sent me, is greater than I. It certainly requires very little argument, and no sophistry, to reconcile this saying with the most orthodox notion of the Godhead of Christ; as he is repeatedly speaking of his Divine and of his human nature. Of the former he says, I and the Father are one, <reference osisRef="Joh.10.30">Joh 10:30</reference>; and of the latter he states, with the same truth, The Father is greater than I.
entries.2a36aee52db13d29aaef20152fe1db2030aa781c: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen42654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42655" type="x-p"/> I have told you before it come to pass - Lest my death should be a stumbling-block to you, I have spoken of it beforehand, and showed you the necessity of it, that when it happens ye may believe, that as I could predict it so clearly, and so circumstantially, so all the good which I have promised shall be the result may be confidently expected by you; and that your sorrow, if not entirely removed, may at least be much mitigated.
entries.cc0b9eb62cf220ea208b573dc70a2723c348759a: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen42655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42656" type="x-p"/> The prince of this world - Τουτου, of this, is omitted by ABDEGHKLMS, Mt. BH, one hundred others; both the Syriac, later Persic, all the Arabic, and several of the primitive fathers. I rather think the omission of the pronoun makes the sense more general; for, had he said This world, the words might have been restrained to the Jewish state, or to the Roman government. But who is the person called here the prince of the world? <div eID="gen42656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42657" type="x-p"/> 1. Mr. Wakefield thinks that Christ speaks here of himself, as he does in <reference osisRef="Joh.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>, (see the note there), and translates this verse and the following thus: For the ruler of this world is coming; and I have nothing now to do, but to convince the world that I love the Father, and do as he commanded me. On which he observes that our Lord speaks of what he shall be, when he comes again, and not of what he then was: compare <reference osisRef="Joh.14.18">Joh 14:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.16.16">Joh 16:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.17.2">Joh 17:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.28.18">Mat 28:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phi.2.9">Phi 2:9</reference>. And how often does he speak of himself, as the Son of man, in the third person! See his vindication of this translation in the third vol. of his New Testament. <div eID="gen42657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42658" type="x-p"/> 2. Others think that our Lord refers to the Roman government, the ruler of the world, who, by its deputy, Pilate, was going to judge him, but who should find nothing (εὑρησει ουδεν, which is the reading found in some excellent MSS. and versions, and is followed by almost all the primitive fathers), as a just cause of death in him - nothing in the whole of his conduct which was in the least reprehensible; and this indeed Pilate witnessed in the most solemn manner. See <reference osisRef="Joh.18.38">Joh 18:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.19.4">Joh 19:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.19.12">Joh 19:12</reference>; see also <reference osisRef="Luk.23.4">Luk 23:4</reference>, etc., and <reference osisRef="Mat.27.24">Mat 27:24</reference>. <div eID="gen42658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42659" type="x-p"/> 3.
