For, though the majesty of God be in itself hidden from us, it shines <hi type="italic">in Christ</hi>; though his hand be concealed, we have it visible <hi type="italic">in Christ</hi>. Consequently, in the benefits which the Father bestows upon us, we have no right to separate <hi type="italic">the Father </hi>from <hi type="italic">the Son</hi>, according to that saying,<div eID="gen106414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106415" type="x-p"/>He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.6.23">John 6:23</reference>.)<div eID="gen106415" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106410" osisID="John.14.13" type="section"/>
entries.7426e4b6b292f10b53c070f1ea4bb6b55f456c48:
14. If you shall ask any thing in my name, I will do it. This is not a useless repetition. All see and feel that they are unworthy to approach God; and yet the greater part of men burst forward, as if they were out of their senses, and rashly and haughtily address God; and afterwards, when that unworthiness, of which I have spoken, comes to their recollection, every man contrives for himself various expedients. On the other hand, when God invites us to himself, he holds out to us one Mediator only, by whom he is willing to be appeased and reconciled. But here again the wickedness of the human mind breaks out for the greater part do not cease to forsake the road, and to pass through many windings. The reason why they do so is, that they have but a poor and slender perception of the power and goodness of God in Christ. To this is added a second error, that we do not consider that we are justly excluded from approaching God, until he calls us, and that we are called only through the Son. And if one passage has not sufficient weight with us, let us know that, when Christ repeats, a second time, that we must pray to the Father in his name, he lays his hand on us, as it were, that we may not lose our pains by fruitlessly seeking other intercessors.
John 14:15-18
15. If you love me, keep my commandments. 16. And I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; 17. The Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, and knoweth him not; but you know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. 18. I will not leave you orphans; I come to you.
“Je viendrai a vous;” — “I will come to you.”
entries.899f6981001ed6af5d285fd856dbfeb08f4826d9: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.15" sID="gen106423" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> <hi type="italic">If you love me.</hi> The <hi type="italic">love </hi>with which the disciples <hi type="italic">loved </hi>Christ was true and sincere, and yet there was some superstition mixed with it, as is frequently the case with ourselves; for it was very foolish in them to wish to keep him in the world. To correct this fault, he bids them direct their love to another end; and that is, to employ themselves in <hi type="italic">keeping the commandments </hi>which he had given them. This is undoubtedly a useful doctrine, for of those who think that they <hi type="italic">love </hi>Christ, there are very few who honor him as they ought to do; but, on the contrary, after having performed small and trivial services, they give themselves no farther concern. The true <hi type="italic">love </hi>of Christ, on the other hand, is regulated by the observation of his doctrine as the only rule. But we are likewise reminded how sinful our affections are, since even the love which we bear to Christ is not without fault, if it be not directed to a pure obedience.<div eID="gen106424" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106423" osisID="John.14.15" type="section"/>
entries.e44c2bef1c61441786bbc56da5adc77977f34dc1: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.16" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.16" sID="gen106425" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> <hi type="italic">And I will pray to the Father.</hi> This was given as a remedy for soothing the grief which they might feel on account of Christ’s absence; but at the same time, Christ promises that he will give them strength <hi type="italic">to keep his commandments</hi>; For otherwise the exhortation would have had little effect. He therefore loses no time in informing them that, though he be absent from them in body, yet he will never allow them to remain destitute of assistance; for he will be present with them by his Spirit.<div eID="gen106426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106427" type="x-p"/>Here he calls the Spirit the gift of <hi type="italic">the Father</hi>, but a gift which he will obtain by his prayers; in another passage he promises that he will give the Spirit. <hi type="italic">If I depart</hi>, says he, <hi type="italic">I will send</hi>,<hi type="italic"> Him to you</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.16.7">John 16:7</reference>.) Both statements are true and correct; for in so far as Christ is our Mediator and Intercessor, he obtains from <hi type="italic">the Father </hi>the grace of the Spirit, but in so far as he is God, he bestows that grace from himself. The meaning of this passage therefore is: “I was given to you by <hi type="italic">the Father </hi>to be <hi type="italic">a Comforter</hi>, but only for a time; now, having discharged my office, I will pray to him to give another <hi type="italic">Comforter</hi>, who will not be for a short time, but will remain always with you.”<div eID="gen106427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106428" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And he will, give you another Comforter.</hi> The word <hi type="italic">Comforter </hi>is here applied both to Christ and to the Spirit, and justly; for it is an office which belongs equally to both of them, to <hi type="italic">comfort </hi>and exhort us, and to guard us by their protection. Christ was the Protector of his disciples, so long as he dwelt in the world: and afterwards he committed them to the protection and guardianship of the Spirit. It may be asked, are we not still under the protection of Christ? The answer is easy. Christ is a continual Protector, but not in a visible way. So long as he dwelt in the world, he openly manifested himself as their Protector; but now he guards us by his Spirit.<div eID="gen106428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106429" type="x-p"/>He calls the Spirit another <hi type="italic">Comforter</hi>, on account of the difference between the blessings which we obtain from both. The peculiar office of Christ was, to appease the wrath of God by atoning for the sins of the world, to redeem men from death, to procure righteousness and life; and the peculiar office of the Spirit is, to make us partakers not only of Christ himself, but of all his blessings. And yet there would be no impropriety in inferring from this passage a distinction of Persons; for there must be some peculiarity in which the Spirit differs from the Son so as to be <hi type="italic">another </hi>than the Son.<div eID="gen106429" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.16" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106425" osisID="John.14.16" type="section"/>
entries.a23c4ce55a4565fdc2c93c596c6d986a24eb5a7f: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.17" sID="gen106430" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> <hi type="italic">The Spirit of truth.</hi> Christ bestows on the Spirit another title, namely, that he is the Master or Teacher of truth. <note n="68"> <div sID="gen106432" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A scavoir qu’il est Maistre ou Docteur de la verite</foreign>.”<div eID="gen106432" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence it follows, that until we have been inwardly instructed by him, the understandings of all of us are seized with vanity and falsehood.<div eID="gen106431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106433" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Whom the world cannot receive.</hi> This contrast shows the peculiar excellence of that grace which God bestows on none but his elect; for he means that it is no ordinary gift of which the world is deprived. In this sense, too, Isaiah says, “<hi type="italic">For</hi>, the darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the people, but the Lord shall arise on thee, O Jerusalem!” <note n="69"> <div sID="gen106434" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sur toy, O Jerusalem</foreign>!”<div eID="gen106434" type="x-p"/> </note> For the mercy of God towards the Church deserves so much the higher praise, when he exalts the Church, by a distinguished privilege, above the whole world. And yet Christ exhorts the disciples, that they must not be puffed up, as the world is wont to be, by carnal views, and thus drive away from themselves the grace of the Spirit. All that Scripture tells us about the Holy Spirit is regarded by earthly men as a dream; because, trusting to their own reason, they despise heavenly illumination. Now, though this pride abounds everywhere, which extinguishes, so far as lies in our power, the light of the Holy Spirit; yet, conscious of our own poverty, we ought to know, that whatever belongs to sound understanding proceeds from no other source. Yet Christ’s words show that nothing which relates to the Holy Spirit can be learned by human reason, but that He is known only by the experience of faith.<div eID="gen106433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106435" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The world</hi>, he says, <hi type="italic">cannot receive the Spirit</hi>,<hi type="italic"> because it knoweth him not</hi>;<hi type="italic"> but you know him</hi>,<hi type="italic"> because he dwelleth with you</hi>. It is the Spirit alone therefore, who, by <hi type="italic">dwelling in us</hi>, makes himself to be known by us, for otherwise, he is unknown and incomprehensible.<div eID="gen106435" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106430" osisID="John.14.17" type="section"/>
entries.9e82667b51100c4d9f9a710af1e01a1f323a5ab5:
18. I will not have you orphans. This passage shows what men are, and what they can do, when they have been deprived of the protection of the Spirit. They are orphans, exposed to every kind of fraud and injustice, incapable of governing themselves, and, in short, unable of themselves to do any thing. The only remedy for so great a defect is, if Christ govern us by his Spirit, which he promises that he will do. First then, the disciples are reminded of their weakness, that, distrusting themselves, they may rely on nothing else than the protection of Christ; and, secondly, having promised a remedy, he gives them good encouragement; for he declares that he will never leave them When he says, I will come to you, he shows in what manner he dwells in his people, and in what manner he fills all things. It is, by the power of his Spirit; and hence it is evident, that the grace of the Spirit is a striking proof of his Divinity.
John 14:19-20
19. Yet a little while, and the world shall see me no more; but you see me: because I live, you also shall live. 20. At that day you shall know that I am in the Father, and you in me, and I in you.
entries.fdd136d10c38a660ca236dfc876fa07210531644: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.19" sID="gen106442" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> <hi type="italic">Yet a little while.</hi> He continues the commendation of special grace, which ought to have been sufficient for alleviating, and even for removing the grief of the disciples. “When I shall have withdrawn,” says he, “from the view of the world: still I shall be present with you.” That we may enjoy this secret beholding of Christ, we must not judge of his presence or his absence according to carnal perception, but we must earnestly employ the eyes of faith for contemplating his power. Thus believers always have Christ present by his Spirit, and behold him, though they be distant from him in body.<div eID="gen106443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106444" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Because I live.</hi> This statement may be explained in two ways. Either it may be viewed as a confirmation of the former clause, <hi type="italic">because I live</hi>,<hi type="italic"> and you shall live</hi>; or, it may be read separately, <hi type="italic">because I live</hi>,<hi type="italic"> you also shall live</hi>; and then the meaning will be, that believers <hi type="italic">will live</hi>,<hi type="italic"> because Christ liveth</hi> I willingly embrace the former opinion, and yet we may draw from it the other doctrine, that the life of Christ is the cause of our life. He begins by pointing out the cause of the difference, why he shall be <hi type="italic">seen </hi>by his disciples, and <hi type="italic">not by the world</hi> It isn’t because Christ cannot be <hi type="italic">seen </hi>but according to the spiritual life, of which the world is deprived. <hi type="italic">The world seeth not </hi>Christ; this is not wonderful, for the death of blindness is the cause; but as soon as any man begins to live by the Spirit, he is immediately endued with eyes to see Christ. Now, the reason of this is, that our life is closely connected with the life of Christ, and proceeds from it as from its source; for we are dead in ourselves, and the life with which we flatter ourselves is a very bad death. Accordingly, when the question is, how we are to obtain life, our eyes must be directed to Christ, and his life must be conveyed to us by faith, that our consciences may be fully convinced, that, so long as Christ lives, we are free from all danger of destruction; for it is an undoubted truth, that <hi type="italic">his life </hi>would be nothing, when his members were dead.<div eID="gen106444" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106442" osisID="John.14.19" type="section"/>
entries.2cbbe1241dab5ff36151f6e3dbe2480bc040dd3f:
20. At that day Some refer this to the day of Pentecost; but it rather denotes the uninterrupted course, as it were, of a single day, from the time when Christ exerted the power of his Spirit till the last resurrection. From that time they began to know, but it was a sort of feeble beginning, because the Spirit had not yet wrought so powerfully in them. For the object of these words is, to show that we cannot, by indolent speculation, know what is the sacred and mystical union between us and him, and again, between him and the Father; but that the only way of knowing it is, when he diffuses his life in us by the secret efficacy of the Spirit; and this is the trial of faith, which I lately mentioned.
As to the manner in which this passage was formerly abused by the Aryans, to prove that Christ is God only by participation and by grace, it is easy to refute their sophistry. For Christ does not speak merely of his eternal essence, but of that Divine power which was manifested in him. As the Father has laid up in the Son all fullness of blessings, so, on the other hand, the Son has conveyed himself entirely into us. He is said to be in us, because he plainly shows, by the efficacy of his Spirit, that he is the Author and the cause of our life.
John 14:21-24
21. He who hath my commandments, and keepeth them, is he that loveth me; and he that loveth me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him. 22. Judas (not Iscariot) saith to him, Lord, why is it
“D’ou vient?” — “Whence comes it?“
that thou wilt manifest thyself to us, and not to the world? 23. Jesus answered and said to him, “If any one love me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our abode with him. 24. He who loveth me not keepeth not my words; and the word which you have heard is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me.”
entries.eddeeaf82e71d3bb45c3d7e27fe72bad97b00f54: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.21" sID="gen106453" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21.</hi> <hi type="italic">He who hath my commandments. He</hi> again repeats the former statement, that the undoubted proof of our love to him lies in our <hi type="italic">keeping his commandments</hi>; and the reason why he so frequently reminds the disciples of this is, that they may not turn aside from this object; for there is nothing to which we are more prone than to slide into a carnal affection, so as to love something else than Christ under the name of Christ. Such is also the import of that saying of Paul,<div eID="gen106454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106455" type="x-p"/>Though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet henceforth we know him no longer in this manner. Let us therefore be a new creature, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.16 Bible:2Cor.5.17">2 Corinthians 5:16, 17</reference>.)<div eID="gen106455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106456" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To have his commandments </hi>means to be properly instructed in them; and <hi type="italic">to </hi>keep <hi type="italic">his commandments </hi>is to conform ourselves and our life to their rule.<div eID="gen106456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106457" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And he that loveth me will be loved by my Father.</hi> Christ speaks as if men loved God before he loved them; which is absurd, for,<div eID="gen106457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106458" type="x-p"/>when we were enemies, he reconciled us to him, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.5.10">Romans 5:10</reference>;)<div eID="gen106458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106459" type="x-p"/>and the words of John are well known,<div eID="gen106459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106460" type="x-p"/>Not that we first loved him, but he first loved us, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1John.4.10">1 John 4:10</reference>.)<div eID="gen106460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106461" type="x-p"/>But there is no debate here about cause or effect; and therefore there is no ground for the inference, that the love with which we love Christ comes in order before the love which God has toward us; for Christ meant only, that all who <hi type="italic">love him </hi>will be happy, because they will also <hi type="italic">be loved by him and by the Father</hi>; not that God then begins to <hi type="italic">love </hi>them, but because they have a testimony of his love to them, as a Father, engraven on their hearts. To the same purpose is the clause which immediately follows: —<div eID="gen106461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106462" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And I will manifest myself to him.</hi> Knowledge undoubtedly goes before love; but Christ’s meaning was, I will grant to those who purely observe my doctrine, that they shall make progress from day to day in faith; “that is, “I will cause them to approach more nearly and more familiarly to <hi type="italic">me</hi>.” Hence infer, that the fruit of piety is progress in the knowledge of Christ; for he who promises that he will give himself to him who has it rejects hypocrites, and causes all to make progress in faith who, cordially embracing the doctrine of the Gospel, bring themselves entirely into obedience to it. And this is the reason why many fall back, and why we scarcely see one in ten proceed in the right course; for the greater part do not deserve that he should <hi type="italic">manifest himself to them</hi> It ought also to be observed, that a more abundant knowledge of Christ is here represented as an extraordinary reward of our love to Christ; and hence it follows that it is an invaluable treasure.<div eID="gen106462" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106453" osisID="John.14.21" type="section"/>
entries.781b8999cd564f3675193d53c7f90d8f04aaca6a: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.22" sID="gen106463" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> <hi type="italic">Judas </hi>(<hi type="italic">not Iscariot</hi>)<hi type="italic"> saith to him.</hi> It is not without reason that he asks why Christ does not cause his light to be imparted <note n="71"> <div sID="gen106465" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pourquoy Christ fera que sa lumiere sera manifestee</foreign>.”<div eID="gen106465" type="x-p"/> </note> to more than a few persons; since he is <hi type="italic">the Sun of Righteousness</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.4.2">Malachi 4:2</reference>) by whom the whole world ought to be enlightened; and, therefore, it is unreasonable that he should enlighten but a few, and not shed his light everywhere without distinction. Christ’s reply does not solve the whole question; for it makes no mention of the first cause, why Christ ‘<hi type="italic">manifested himself to </hi>a few,’ conceals himself from the greater part of men; for certainly he finds all men at first alike, that is, entirely alienated from him; and, therefore, he cannot choose any person who loves him, but he chooses from among his enemies those whose hearts he bends to the love of him. But he did not intend, at present, to take any notice of that distinction, which was far from the object he had in view. His design was, to exhort his disciples to the earnest study of godliness, that they might make greater progress in faith; and, therefore, he is satisfied with distinguishing them from the world by this mark, that they keep the doctrine of the Gospel.<div eID="gen106464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106466" type="x-p"/>Now, this mark comes after the commencement of faith, for it is the effect of their calling. In other passages, Christ had reminded the disciples of their being called by free grace, and he will afterwards bring it to their recollection. At present, he only enjoins them to observe his doctrine, and to maintain godliness. By these words, Christ shows in what manner the Gospel is properly obeyed. It is, when our services and outward actions proceed from the love of Christ; for in vain do the arms, and the feet, and the whole body toil, if the love of God does not reign in the heart, to govern the outward members. Now, since it is certain that we <hi type="italic">keep the commandments </hi>of Christ only in so far as we <hi type="italic">love </hi>him, it follows that a perfect <hi type="italic">love </hi>of him can nowhere be found in the world, because there is no man who <hi type="italic">keeps his commandments </hi>perfectly; yet God is pleased with the obedience of those who sincerely aim at this end.<div eID="gen106466" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106463" osisID="John.14.22" type="section"/>
entries.0a0d81f20d4ed70faaaea1573751230ad8a5a12e: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.23" sID="gen106467" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23.</hi> <hi type="italic">And my Father will love him.</hi> We have already explained that the love of God to us is not placed in the second rank, as if it came after our piety as the cause of that love, but that believers may be fully convinced that the obedience which they render to the Gospel is pleasing to God, and that they may continually expect from him fresh additions of gifts.<div eID="gen106468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106469" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And we will come to him who loveth me;</hi> that is, he will feel that the grace of God dwelleth in him, and will every day receive additions to the gifts of God. He therefore speaks, not of that eternal love with which he loved us, before we were born, and even before the world was created, but since the time when he seals it on our hearts by making us partakers of his adoption. Nor does he even mean the first illumination, but those degrees of faith by which believers must continually advance, according to that saying,<div eID="gen106469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106470" type="x-p"/>Whosoever hath it shall be given to him, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.12">Matthew 13:12</reference>.)<div eID="gen106470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106471" type="x-p"/>The Papists; therefore are wrong in inferring from this passage that there are two kinds of love with which we love God. They falsely maintain that we naturally love God, before he regenerates us by his Spirit, and even that by this preparation we merit the grace of regeneration; as if Scripture did not everywhere teach, and as if experience also did not loudly proclaim, that we are altogether alienated from God, and that we are infected and filled with hatred of him, until he change our hearts. We must therefore keep in view the design of Christ, that he <hi type="italic">and the Father will come</hi>, to confirm believers, in uninterrupted confidence in his grace.<div eID="gen106471" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106467" osisID="John.14.23" type="section"/>
entries.a432eb863a8bd1bea3ebb98e6cfae74991506b79:
24. He who loveth, me but keepeth not my words. As believers are mixed with unbelievers in the world, and as they must be agitated by various storms, as in a troubled sea, Christ again confirms them by this admonition, that they may not be drawn away by bad examples. As if he had said, “Do not look upon the world so as to depend on it; for there will always be some who despise me and my doctrine; but as for you, preserve constantly to the end the grace which you have once received.” Yet he likewise intimates that the world is justly punished for its ingratitude, when it perishes in its blindness, since, by despising true righteousness, it manifests a wicked hatred towards Christ.
And the word which you hear. That the disciples may not be discouraged or waver on account of the obstinacy of the world, he again procures credit to his doctrine, by testifying that it is from God, and that it was not contrived by men on the earth. And, indeed, the strength of our faith consists in our knowing that God is our leader, and that we are founded on nothing else than his eternal truth. Whatever then may be the rage and madness of the world, let us follow the doctrine of Christ, which rises far above heaven and earth. When he says that the word is not his, he accommodates himself to the disciples; as if he had said that it is not human, because he teaches faithfully what has been enjoined on him by the Father. Yet we know that, in so far as he is the eternal Wisdom of God, he is the only fountain of all doctrine, and that all the prophets who have been from the beginning spoke by his Spirit.
John 14:25-28
25. These things I have spoken to you, while I remain with you. 26. But the Comforter, (who is
“(Qui est) le Sainct Esprit.”
) the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and will bring to your remembrance all things that I have said to you. 27. Peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you: not as the world giveth, give I it to you.
“Et je ne la vous donne point, comme le monde la donne;” — “and I give it not to you, as the world giveth it.”
Let not your heart be troubled, and let it not be afraid. 28. You heard that I said to you, I go away, and come to you. If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice that I said, I go to the Father; for the Father is greater than I.
entries.bf616c8fe8185ab0b890f8fd838b2107cb1c1e35: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.25" sID="gen106481" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> <hi type="italic">These things I have spoken to you.</hi> He adds this, that they may not despair, though they may have profited less than they ought to have done; for at that time he scattered a seed of doctrine, which lay hidden, and, as it were, suffocated in the disciples. He therefore exhorts them to entertain good hopes, until fruit be yielded by the doctrine which might now appear to be useless. In short, he testifies that in the doctrine which they had heard they have abundant ground of consolation, and that they ought not to seek it anywhere else. And if they do not immediately see it, he bids them be of good courage, until the Holy Spirit, who is the inward Teacher, speak the same thing in their hearts. This admonition is highly useful to all; for, if we do not immediately understand what Christ teaches, we begin to grow weary, and grudge to bestow unprofitable labor on what is obscure. But we must bring an eager desire to receive instruction; we must lend our ears and give attention, if we desire to make due proficiency in the school of God; and especially we need patience, until the Holy Spirit enable us to understand what we thought that we had often read or heard to no purpose. That the desire of learning may not be weakened in us, or that we may not fall into despair, when we do not immediately perceive the meaning of Christ speaking to us, let us know that this is spoken to us all.<div eID="gen106482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106483" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The Holy Spirit will bring to your remembrance all things that I have said to you.</hi> It is indeed a punishment threatened by Isaiah against unbelievers, that the Word of God shall be to them <hi type="italic">as a book that is sealed</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.29.11">Isaiah 29:11</reference>) but in this manner, also, the Lord frequently humbles his people. We ought, therefore, to wait patiently and mildly for the time of revelation, and must not, on that account, reject the word. When Christ testifies that it is the peculiar office of the Holy Spirit to teach the apostles what they had already learned from his mouth, it follows that the outward preaching will be vain and useless, if it be not accompanied by the teaching of the Spirit. God has therefore two ways of teaching; for, <hi type="italic">first</hi>, he sounds in our ears by the mouth of men; and, <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, he addresses us inwardly by his Spirit; and he does this either at the same moment, or at different times, as he thinks fit.<div eID="gen106483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106484" type="x-p"/>But observe what are <hi type="italic">all these things </hi>which he promises that the Spirit will teach. <hi type="italic">He will suggest</hi>, he says, <hi type="italic">or bring to your remembrance</hi>, <hi type="italic">all that I have said</hi>. Hence it follows, that he will not be a builder of new revelations. By this single word we may refute all the inventions which Satan has brought into the Church from the beginning, under the pretense of the Spirit. Mahomet and the Pope agree in holding this as a principle of their religion, that Scripture does not contain a perfection of doctrine, but that something loftier has been revealed by the Spirit. From the same point the Anabaptists and Libertines, in our own time, have drawn their absurd notions. But the spirit that introduces any doctrine or invention apart from the Gospel is a deceiving spirit, and not the Spirit of Christ. What is meant by <hi type="italic">the Spirit being sent by the Father in the name of Christ</hi>, I have already explained.<div eID="gen106484" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106481" osisID="John.14.25" type="section"/>
entries.c3416d26add8a972bafa9438e51e5af2dc127b07: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.27" sID="gen106485" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi> <hi type="italic">Peace I leave with you.</hi> By the word<hi type="italic"> peace </hi>he means prosperity, which men are wont to wish for each other when they meet or part; for such is the import of the word <hi type="italic">peace </hi>in the Hebrew language. He therefore alludes to the ordinary custom of his nation; as if he had said, <hi type="italic">I give you my Farewell</hi> But he immediately adds, that this <hi type="italic">peace </hi>is of far greater value than that which is usually to be found among men, who generally have the word <hi type="italic">peace </hi>but coldly in their mouth, by way of ceremony, or, if they sincerely wish <hi type="italic">peace </hi>for any one, yet cannot actually bestow it. But Christ reminds them that <hi type="italic">his peace </hi>does not consist in an empty and unavailing wish, but is accompanied by the effect. In short, he says that he goes away from them in body, but that <hi type="italic">his peace </hi>remains with the disciples; that is, that they will be always happy through his blessing.<div eID="gen106486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106487" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Let not your heart be troubled.</hi> He again corrects the alarm which the disciples had felt on account of his departure. It is no ground for alarm, he tells them; for they want only his bodily presence, but will enjoy his actual presence through the Spirit. Let us learn to be always satisfied with this kind of presence, and let us not give a loose reign to the flesh, which always binds God by its outward inventions.<div eID="gen106487" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106485" osisID="John.14.27" type="section"/>
entries.1dcc590cd10a8dd7393a08f739d7a8a4ebc4f874:
28. If you loved me you would rejoice. The disciples unquestionably loved Christ, but not as they ought to have done; for some carnal affection was mixed with their love, so that they could not endure to be separated from him; but if they had loved him spiritually, there was nothing which they would have had more deeply at heart, than his return to the Father.
For the Father is greater than I. This passage has been tortured in various ways. The Aryans, in order to prove that Christ is some sort of inferior God, argued that he is less than the Father The orthodox Fathers, to remove all ground for such a calumny, said that this must have referred to his human nature; but as the Aryans wickedly abused this testimony, so the reply given by the Fathers to their objection was neither correct nor appropriate; for Christ does not now speak either of his human nature, or of his eternal Divinity, but, accommodating himself to our weakness, places himself between God and us; and, indeed, as it has not been granted to us to reach the height of God, Christ descended to us, that he might raise us to it. You ought to have rejoiced, he says, because I return to the Father; for this is the ultimate object at which you ought to aim. By these words he does not show in what respect he differs in himself from the Father, but why he descended to us; and that was that he might unite us to God; for until we have reached that point, we are, as it were, in the middle of the course. We too imagine to ourselves but a half-Christ, and a mutilated Christ, if he do not lead us to God.
There is a similar passage in the writings of Paul, where he says that Christ
will deliver up the Kingdom to God his Father, that God may be all in all, (1 Corinthians 15:24.)
Christ certainly reigns, not only in human nature, but as he is God manifested in the flesh. In what manner, therefore, will he lay aside the kingdom? It is, because the Divinity which is now beheld in Christ’s face alone, will then be openly visible in him. The only point of difference is, that Paul there describes the highest perfection of the Divine brightness, the rays of which began to shine from the time when Christ ascended to heaven. To make the matter more clear, we must use still greater plainness of speech. Christ does not here make a comparison between the Divinity of the Father and his own, nor between his own human nature and the Divine essence of the Father, but rather between his present state and the heavenly glory, to which he would soon afterwards be received; as if he had said, “You wish to detain me in the world, but it is better that I should ascend to heaven.” Let us therefore learn to behold Christ humbled in the flesh, so that he may conduct us to the fountain of a blessed immortality; for he was not appointed to be our guide, merely to raise us to the sphere of the moon or of the sun, but to make us one with God the Father.
John 14:29-31
29. And I have told you now, before it take place, that, when it shall take place, you may believe. 30. Henceforth I will not talk much with you: for the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me. 31. But that the world may know that I love the Father, and that I do as the Father hath commanded me. Arise, let us go hence.
entries.60906e548b9a243e6b77dbc4edcd4f0732fd66b5: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.29" sID="gen106498" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi> <hi type="italic">And I have told you now.</hi> It was proper that the disciples should be frequently admonished on this point; for it was a secret far exceeding all human capacity. He testifies that he <hi type="italic">foretells what shall happen</hi>,<hi type="italic"> that</hi>,<hi type="italic"> when it has happened</hi>,<hi type="italic"> they may believe</hi>; for it was a useful confirmation of their faith when they brought to recollection the predictions of Christ, and saw accomplished before their eyes what they had formerly heard from his mouth. Yet it appears to be a sort of concession, as if Christ had said, “Because you are not yet capable of comprehending so deep a mystery, I bear with you till the event has happened, which will serve as an interpreter to explain this doctrine.” Although for a time he seemed to speak to the deaf, yet it afterwards appeared that his words were not scattered in vain, or, as we may say, in the air, but that it was a seed thrown into the earth. Now, as Christ speaks here about his word and the accomplishment of events, so his death, and resurrection, and ascension to heaven, are combined with doctrine, that they may produce faith in us.<div eID="gen106499" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106498" osisID="John.14.29" type="section"/>
entries.b6464fc83f96c89184b1fbdb5b18622ac14f49a7: <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="John.14.30" sID="gen106500" type="section"/> <div sID="gen106501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30.</hi> <hi type="italic">Henceforth I will not talk much with you.</hi> By this word he intended to fix the attention of the disciples on himself, and to impress his doctrine more deeply on their minds; for abundance generally takes away the appetite, and we desire more eagerly what we have not in our possession, and delight more in the enjoyment of that which is speedily to be taken from us. In order, therefore, to make them more desirous of hearing his doctrines, he threatens that he will very soon go away. Although Christ does not cease to teach us during the whole course of our life, yet this statement may be applied to our use; for, since the course of our life is short, we ought to embrace the present opportunity.<div eID="gen106501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106502" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For the prince of this world cometh</hi> He might have said, in direct language, that he would soon die, and that the hour of his death was at hand; but he makes use of a circumlocution, to fortify their minds beforehand, lest, terrified by a kind of death so hideous and detestable, they should faint; for to believe in him crucified, what is it but to seek life in hell? First, he says that his power will be given to Satan; and next he adds, That he will go away, not because he is compelled to do so, but in order to obey the Father.<div eID="gen106502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106503" type="x-p"/>The devil is called <hi type="italic">the prince of this world,</hi> not because he has a kingdom separated from God, (as the Manicheans imagined,) but because, by God’s permission, he exercises his tyranny over the world. Whenever, therefore, we hear this designation applied to the devil, let us be ashamed of our miserable condition; for, whatever may be the pride of men, they are the slaves of the devil, till they are regenerated by the Spirit of Christ; for under the term <hi type="italic">world </hi>is here included the whole human race. There is but one Deliverer who frees and rescues us from this dreadful slavery. Now, since this punishment was inflicted on account of the sin of the first man, and since it daily grows worse on account of new sins, let us learn to hate both ourselves and our sins. While we are held captives under the dominion of Satan, still this slavery does not free us from blame, for it is voluntary. It ought also to be observed, that what is done by wicked men is here ascribed to the devil; for, since they are impelled by Satan, all that they do is justly reckoned his work.<div eID="gen106503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen106504" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And hath nothing in me.</hi> <note n="74"> <div sID="gen106505" type="x-p"/> This is the literal rendering of <foreign xml:lang="el">καὶ ἐν ἐμοὶ οὐκ ἔχει οὐδὲν</foreign> and corresponds to other modern versions; as, for example, the German, <foreign xml:lang="de">und hat nichts an mir</foreign>; though Wolffus quotes a marginal reading of a German translation, <foreign xml:lang="de">an mir wird er nicht nichts unden</foreign>, — <hi type="italic">he will find nothing in me</hi>. The latter agrees with a Greek reading <foreign xml:lang="el">καὶ ἐν ἐμοὶ οὐχ εὑρήσει οὐδὲν</foreign> <hi type="italic">and will</hi> find <hi type="italic">nothing in me</hi>; and. with another reading <foreign xml:lang="el">καὶ ἐν ἐμοὶ οὐκ ἔχει οὐδὲν εὑρεῖν</foreign>, <hi type="italic">and hath nothing to</hi> find <hi type="italic">in me</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen106505" type="x-p"/> </note> It is in consequence of the sin of Adam that Satan holds the dominion of death, and, therefore, he could not touch Christ, who is pure from all the pollution of sin, if he had not voluntarily subjected himself. And yet I think that these words have a wider meaning than that in which they are usually explained; for the ordinary interpretation is, “Satan hath found nothing in Christ, for there is nothing in him that deserves death, because he is pure from every stain of sin.” But, in my opinion, Christ asserts here not only his own purity, but likewise his Divine power, which was not subject to death; for it was proper to assure the disciples that he did not yield through weakness, lest they should think less highly of his power. But in this general statement the former is also included, that, in enduring death, he was not compelled by Satan. Hence we infer, that he was substituted in our room, when he submitted to death.<div eID="gen106504" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:John.14.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen106500" osisID="John.14.30" type="section"/>
entries.432c893d488f6c4b0ae0c00ec5e94a1443e2f3e0:
31. But that the world may know. Some think that these words should be read as closely connected with the words, Arise, let us go hence, so as to make the sense complete. Others read the former part of the verse separately, and suppose that it breaks off abruptly. As it makes no great difference in regard to the meaning, I leave it to the reader to give a preference to either of these views. What chiefly deserves our attention is, that the decree of God is here placed in the highest rank; that we may not suppose that Christ was dragged to death by the violence of Satan, in such a manner that anything happened contrary to the purpose of God. It was God who appointed his Son to be the Propitiation, and who determined that the sins of the world should be expiated by his death. In order to accomplish this, he permitted Satan, for a short time, to treat him with scorn; as if he had gained a victory over him. Christ, therefore, does not resist Satan, in order that he may obey the decree of his Father, and may thus offer his obedience as the ransom of our righteousness.
Arise, let us go hence. Some think that Christ, after he said these things, changed his place, and that what follows was spoken by him on the road; but as John afterwards adds, that Christ went away with his disciples beyond the brook Kedron,
“Que Christ s’en alla avec ses disciples outre le torrent de Cedron.”
it appears more probable that Christ intended to exhort the disciples to render the same obedience to God, of which they beheld in him so illustrious an example, and not that he led them away at that moment.
Chapter 15
John 15:1-6
1. I am the true Vine, and my Father is the Husbandman. 2. Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he will take away, and every branch that beareth fruit he will prune, that it may bear more fruit. 3. You are already clean, on account of the word which I have spoken to you. 4. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless it abide in the vine, so neither can you, unless you abide in me. 5. I am the Vine, you are the branches. He who abideth in me, and I in him, beareth much fruit; for without me you can do nothing. 6. If any one abide not in me, he shall be cast out, and wither as a branch; and men shall gather it, and cast it into the fire, and it shall be burned.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="14" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. XIV.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p>The three ensuing Chapters, continue either one or more consolatory discourses of our Saviour to his Disciples, (as ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peareth from the first verse of this Chapter) made as is pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable to them in the guest chamber; (at least that part of them which we have in this Chapter) for we read of no mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of our Saviours, till we come to the last verse of this Chap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter. That which troubled them was, what he had told them in the close of the former Chapter, that he was going from them; By our Saviours discourse in this and the two following Chapters, it should seem that there were three things that troubled them. <ns0:hi>1.</ns0:hi> The sense of their loss as to his bodily pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sence. <ns0:hi>2.</ns0:hi> The fear, that with the loss of that, they should also lose those Spiritual influences which they had received from him, and upon which their Souls had lived. <ns0:hi>3.</ns0:hi> The prospect of those storms of troubles, and persecutions, which was like to follow his departure from them; for if we wisely consider what our Saviour saith in these three following Chapters, it all tends to comfort them as to troubles that might arise in their spirits, upon one or other of these accounts: the ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neral Proposition is laid down in the first verse of this Chap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:argument>
               <ns0:p>LEt not your hearts be troubled <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Through <ns0:hi>grief,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>fear,</ns0:hi> which are the Two Passions which ordinarily most disturb our minds; our Saviour him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self was troubled, but not sinfully: his trouble neither a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rose from unbelief, nor yet was in an undue measure: it was (as one well expresseth it) like the meer agitation of clear water, where was no mud at the bottom; but our trouble is like the stirring of water that hath a great deal of mu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> at the bottom, which upon the royling, riseth up, and ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />keth the whole body of the water in the vessel impure, ro<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>l<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed and muddy. It is this sinful trouble caused from these Two passions, and rising up to an immoderate degree, and mixed with a great deal of unbelief and distrust in God, a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst which our Saviour here cautioneth his Disciples; and the Remedy he prescribes against those afflicting passions, is a believing in God, and a believing on him.</ns0:note>: ye believe in God <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Two latter passages in the Verse, are so penned in the <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> that they may be read Four ways; for the Verb <ns0:hi>Believe,</ns0:hi> twice repeated, may be read either indicatively or imparitively, or the one may be read <ns0:hi>indicatively,</ns0:hi> and the other <ns0:hi>imperatively</ns0:hi>; so as they may be translated, <ns0:hi>You believe in God, you be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve also in me.</ns0:hi> And so they teach us, that there is no such Remedy for inward troubles, as a believing in God, and a believing in Jesus Christ; and those that do so, have no just Reason for any excessive heart-troubles. Or else they may be read, <ns0:hi>believe in God, believe in me:</ns0:hi> or else as we read them, <ns0:hi>ye believe in God, believe also in me</ns0:hi>: or <ns0:hi>believe in God, ye believe in me.</ns0:hi> But the Disciples Faith in Christ, as Mediator, and God-Man, being yet weak, and their weak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness being what our Saviour hath ordinarily blamed, not magnified, or commended, the best Interpreters judg the sense which our Translators give, to be the best sense; and judg that our Saviour doth inculcate to them his Divine Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, and again offer himself to them as the proper Object of their Faith. You (saith he) own it for your duty to trust in God, as your Creator, and he that provideth for you.</ns0:note>, believe also in me <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Believe also in me,</ns0:hi> as God equal with my Father; and in me, as the Messiah, your Mediator and Redeemer; so as you have one to take care of all your concerns, both those of your Bodies, and those of your Souls also, so as you have nothing to be immoderately, and excessively, or distrustfully troubled for; therefore <ns0:hi>Let not your hearts be troubled</ns0:hi>; onely without care or distust, commit your selves to me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:359" />2 In my Fathers house are many mansions <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Our Lord's first Argument brought to comfort them from the place whither he was going, and the end of his going thither; the place whither he was going, was his <ns0:hi>Fathers house,</ns0:hi> so as they needed not to be troubled for him, he was but going home; nor was God his Father onely, but theirs also, as he afterwards saith, <ns0:hi>I go to my Father, and your Father</ns0:hi>; and here he tells them, that in his Fathers house there was not onely a mansion that is, an abiding place for him, but for many others also. <ns0:hi>Our days on the Earth</ns0:hi> (saith <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>) 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 29.15. <ns0:hi>are as a shadow,</ns0:hi> and there is no abiding; but in Heaven there are <ns0:gap reason="foreign">

                     </ns0:gap>, abiding places. We shall (saith the Apostle) <ns0:hi>be ever with the Lord</ns0:hi>: and the Mansions there, are many; there is room enough for all believers. I would not have deceived you; if there had been no place in heaven but for me, I would have told you of it; but there are many Mansions there.</ns0:note>; if <ns0:hi>it were</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>so,</ns0:hi> I would have told you: I go to pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pare a place for you <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>I go to prepare a place for you.</ns0:hi> The place was prepared of old; those who shall be saved, were of old ordained unto life. That <ns0:hi>King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom was prepared for them before the foundation of the world</ns0:hi> (that is, in the counsels and immutable purpose of God) These Mansions for believers in Heaven, were to be sprinkled with blood: The sprinkling of the <ns0:hi>Tabernacle,</ns0:hi> and all the <ns0:hi>Vessels of the Ministry,</ns0:hi> were typical of it, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9.21, 22, 23. but <ns0:hi>the heavenly things themselves, with bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter sacrifices than these,</ns0:hi> saith the <ns0:hi>Apostle.</ns0:hi> By his Resurre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction from the dead, and becoming the First Fruits of those that sleep; by his Ascension into Heaven, as our forerunner, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6.20. by his <ns0:hi>sitting at the right hand of God,</ns0:hi> and making intercession for us, he prepareth for us a place in Heaven.                <ns0:p n="16">16 And I will pray the Father, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15.26. Rom. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>.25, 26.</ns0:note> he shall give you another Comforter <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This Verse containeth a new Argument by which our <ns0:hi>Saviour</ns0:hi> relieveth his Disciples under their affliction for the want of his bodily presence; that is, the Mission of the Holy Spirit, <ns0:hi>another Comforter</ns0:hi> (as our Translation reads it); For this he saith, that <ns0:hi>he will pray the Father</ns0:hi>; not that himself had no concern in the Mission of the Blessed Spirit; for himself telleth us, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 16.7. that <ns0:hi>he would send him,</ns0:hi> only for the attestation of his Humane Nature; and 2. <ns0:hi>Of himself,</ns0:hi> as our Mediator: 3. <ns0:hi>Of his Father's con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cern as well as his own, in sending the Holy Spirit</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> he here saith, <ns0:hi>I will pray the Father, and he shall send you another comforter.</ns0:hi> That term, <ns0:hi>another,</ns0:hi> signifieth the <ns0:hi>per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonal distinction of the Third</ns0:hi> from the <ns0:hi>First</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Second Person</ns0:hi> in the blessed <ns0:hi>Trinity.</ns0:hi> And the name here given to the <ns0:hi>blessed Spirit,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> (which we too narrowly translate <ns0:hi>Comforter</ns0:hi>), is a term exceeding proper to signifie all the Operations of the blessed Spirit in and upon the souls of his people. The same word, 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.2. where it is ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plied to Christ (as here it is to the Spirit), is there much bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter translated <ns0:hi>Advocate</ns0:hi>; and it is most probable that our Translators here translate it <ns0:hi>Comforter,</ns0:hi> because he is here promised to the Disciples troubled, as fitted to their present distress. The Verb from whence the word deriveth, signifies not to <ns0:hi>comfort</ns0:hi> only, but to <ns0:hi>exhort,</ns0:hi> and to <ns0:hi>be an Advocate</ns0:hi> for another. Now it belongs to the Office of an <ns0:hi>Advocate</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>suggesi</ns0:hi> to his Client what may be for his advantage; which is also the Office of the blessed Spirit; <ns0:hi>if he seeth his Client in an error,</ns0:hi> to reprove, and to convince him; which is also the work of the Spirit, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 6.7. If he seeth him weak, and discouraged, to <ns0:hi>uphold, strengthen,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>encourage him</ns0:hi>; this is also the Spirit's work, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 3.16. if he sees him run<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning into an error, to <ns0:hi>restrain him</ns0:hi>; if he finds him <ns0:hi>dull, and heavy,</ns0:hi> to quicken him; if he seeth him ready to be run<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />down, to <ns0:hi>defend him</ns0:hi>; if he hath any thing to do in the Court, to <ns0:hi>prepare, and dram it up for him,</ns0:hi> and as occasion serveth, to <ns0:hi>speak for him.</ns0:hi> All these things (as might be largely shewed) fall within the Office of an <ns0:hi>Advocate,</ns0:hi> and under the comprehensive term here used.</ns0:note>, that he may abide with you for ever <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">And (saith our Saviour) <ns0:hi>he shall abide with you for ever.</ns0:hi> I shall be with you but for a while, but he shall abide with you to <ns0:hi>eternity</ns0:hi> (as some observe this word is constantly used by this Evange<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />list). So that the <ns0:hi>Promise of the Spirit</ns0:hi> is not to be restrain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed only to the Apostles and their Successors in the Ministry, or to be understood only of those extraordinary gifts be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stowed on the Apostles, and first Ministers of the Gospel; but to be extended further, both with reference to <ns0:hi>persons</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>influences</ns0:hi>; and without doubt the influences of the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit, both as to <ns0:hi>Gifts</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Graces,</ns0:hi> both upon <ns0:hi>Ministers</ns0:hi> and more private <ns0:hi>Christians,</ns0:hi> are much more plentiful since the sending of the Holy Ghost, after Christ's Ascension in the <ns0:hi>days of Pentecost,</ns0:hi> than ever they were before, not as to par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticular persons, a <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>: Or some particular per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons might have greater measures than any, or the most have since had: but as to the generality of Ministers, and Christians, doubtless, since the pouring out of the Spirit in the days of Pentecost, there have been greater measures of the Gifts and Graces of the Holy Spirit given out, and will be to the end of the World, than ever was in any Age before Christ's Ascension, which is no more than what was prophesied, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 44.3. <ns0:hi>Ioel</ns0:hi> 2.28. applied to the days of <ns0:hi>Pentecost, Acts</ns0:hi> 2.17. but not to be limited to that time or age, either for gifts or gracious habits, for as the extraordinary gifts and pow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers, held in some degree after the Apostles age, (if we may give any credit to Ecclesiastical history) so both in those ages, and e<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>er since, as to the generality both of Ministers and Christians, (that is, such as are mentioned <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15. <ns0:hi>that love Christ, and keep his commandments</ns0:hi>) there have been fuller measures of gifts, of more constant standing use for the Church, such as those of <ns0:hi>Knowledge</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Vtterance, &c.</ns0:hi> and also of inward graces, than ever before was.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>

This love of God is the cause, not the effect of our obedience; but <ns0:hi>love</ns0:hi> in this verse must be expounded by <ns0:hi>manifesting</ns0:hi> in the former verse; and this is certain, that the manifestations of Divine love to our Souls, depend upon our walking with God.</ns0:note>: and my Father will love him <ns0:hi>f,</ns0:hi> and we will come unto him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This is also meant by God the Father, and Christs <ns0:hi>coming</ns0:hi> to those that love him, and keep his commandments; <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> a coming in the sweet influences of Divine grace, suted to the Souls va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious necessities:</ns0:note>, and make our abode with him <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">nay, our Lord promiseth, not onely his and his Fathers coming to, but their making an <ns0:hi>abode</ns0:hi> with such as <ns0:hi>love him,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>keep his Commandments.</ns0:hi> Here the abiding of the first and second person in the Trinity with Believers, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 16. the abiding of the third person with them is also promised, which all make that presence of God with them, so often promised to them in holy Writ: Thus our Saviour answereth one part of what <ns0:hi>Iudas said, How is it that thou wilt manifest thy self to us</ns0:hi>? because saith our Saviour, you love me and keep my words; for tho no love, no works of ours foreseen or seen, be the cause of eternal love, or the first grace; yet it is so much a cause of further grace, especially in the sensible manifestations of it, that no Soul must expect it that doth not love Christ, and keep his words. He also further gives them a reason, as to the second thing he asked, why he did not manifest himself to the World?</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:361" />24 He that loveth me not, keepeth not my say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Because they did not love him, nor keep his sayings, their sin was aggravated; because</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 5.19. ver. 10.</ns0:note> the word which you hear is not mine <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">the words which he spake, were not his Will onely,</ns0:note>
                  <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but the Fathers which sent me <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">but the will of his Father who had sent him into the World, to reveal his Will to the Sons of men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 These things have I spoken unto you, being yet present with you <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">That is, as to his bodily presence: for more than three years I have been fulfilling a ministry amongst you, and have spoken many things to you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 But the Comforter, <ns0:hi>which is</ns0:hi> the holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my Name <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The word is the same, which was so translated before; (see the import of it, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 16, 17) he is either called the <ns0:hi>Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />forter,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Spirit of truth</ns0:hi> here, the <ns0:hi>Holy Spirit.</ns0:hi> The Father here is said to send in the name, that is, with the <ns0:hi>Au<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thority,</ns0:hi> and upon the Mediation of the Lord Jesus Christ: and two pieces of the Spirits work besides <ns0:hi>Comforting,</ns0:hi> are here expressed.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 16.13. 1 Joh. 2.20, 27.</ns0:note> he shall teach you all things <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He shall more fully explain to you all things: three of the Apostles themselves had already in this Chapter discovered great degrees of ignorance as to the Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine of the Trinity, Christs Union or Oneness with his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> You shall not be left (saith our Saviour) in this ignorance; for when the holy Spirit shall come, he shall more fully and perfectly instruct you in all things, which I have al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ready instructed you, and which are necessary for you to know in order to your eternal happiness:</ns0:note>, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to you <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">and shall bring to your remembrance the things I have taught you, so as you shall more fully and clearly understand them; and tho you may have forgotten them, yet they shall by the holy Spirit be received in your memories, so as they shall not be like water spilt on the ground, which cannot again be gathered up, but like seed sown in the Earth, which tho it may at present rot, and die under the clods, or at least not Spring up; yet it shall spring up, and bring forth desired fruit. It is one great work of the holy Spirit, to bring the revelations of holy Writ to our remembrance, and withall to clear to us the sense of them, and confirm our faith in them, and chiefly quicken us to practice what is our duty: but it is to be observed, that the Spirit doth not make revelations of new Notions; it onely brings to our remembrance what Christ hath said, and further revealeth what was before in the word revealed, tho possibly particular persons were ig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />norant of such revelations of the word: so things may be new, and newly revealed to us, which in themselves are not so. There are no new truths, but particular persons may have new discoveries of old truth, which they had before misappr<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ensions of.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Peace I leave with you <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Peace be with you, or to you, was the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> common salutation, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 25.6. under that general name, they comprehend all manner of good: With this good wish they both saluted their friends when they met them, and took their farewell of them when they left them. Christ being now about to take his leave for a time of his Disciples, wish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth them <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi>; nay, he doth not onely wish it to them, but he <ns0:hi>leaves</ns0:hi> it to them, he giveth it them as a legacy, and that in another kind of peace, and in another manner than was common</ns0:note>, my peace I give unto you <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">He therefore calls it <ns0:hi>his Peace</ns0:hi> revealed in the Gospel, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.15. purchased with his blood, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 5.1. brought to the Soul by his Spirit, by which we are sealed to the day of Redemption: Christs peace is either Union, or Reconciliation with God, or the copy of it, which is a quiet of conscience, and assurance of his love: Or an union with men by <ns0:hi>Brotherly</ns0:hi> love, so often commended and pressed by Christ.</ns0:note>: not as the world giveth, give I unto you <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Nor doth Christ give this peace as the men of the World giveth peace, who often wish peace earnestly, never considering what it is they say; often, falsly, formally wish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing peace, when they are about to strike those to whom they wish it, under the fifth rib, and when they are most se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious with it, but cannot give it: Christ leaves it to his Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples for a legacy, giveth it to them as a gift; if they want it, it is their own fault; therefore</ns0:note>. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">as in the first verse, so here again, he saith, <ns0:hi>Let not your heart be troubled</ns0:hi>; and adds, <ns0:hi>nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther let it be afraid. Fear</ns0:hi> is one of those passions which most usually and potently doth disturb the hearts and minds of men; but there was no reason it should have this ill influ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence on Christs Disciples, because he had left them <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> for his legacy, and the gifts of God are without <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>epentance; and <ns0:hi>if God be for us,</ns0:hi> saith the Apostle, who, or what can be a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst us?</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 Ye have heard how <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 18.</ns0:note> I said unto you, I go away, and come <ns0:hi>again</ns0:hi> unto you <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">They had heard our Saviour saying so, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 3.</ns0:note>. If ye loved me, ye would rejoyce, because I said, I go unto the Father <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">It is of the nature of true love, to rejoice in the good of the ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ject beloved, as much as in its own, nay before its own; (saith our Saviour) <ns0:hi>if you loved me,</ns0:hi> that is, as ye ought to love me, for our Lord had before owned, that they did love him, giving it as a reason why he rather revealed himself, and manifested himself to them, than to the World, (<ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 23) you would (saith our Saviour) not have been so unreasonably disturbed at my telling you, that I shall leave you; because I not onely told you, that I would come again to you, but because I told you, that I was <ns0:hi>going to my Father, ver.</ns0:hi> 2. from whom tho I was never separated, as I am God over all blessed for ever<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> yet my <ns0:hi>human Nature</ns0:hi> was yet never glori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied with him, so that I shall be there much happier than here; being <ns0:hi>highly exalted,</ns0:hi> and having a <ns0:hi>name given me above every name, Phil.</ns0:hi> 2.10</ns0:note>: for my Father is greater than I <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">For <ns0:hi>my Father is greater than I</ns0:hi>; not greater in <ns0:hi>Essence,</ns0:hi> (as the <ns0:hi>Arrians</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Socini<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ns</ns0:hi> would have it): he had many times before asserted the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trary; but greater, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Either as the order amongst the Divine persons, because the Father begat, the Son is begotte<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>; the Father is he from whom the Son proceeded by <ns0:hi>Eternal gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration</ns0:hi>: in which sense, divers of the Ancients, amongst whom <ns0:hi>Athanasius, Cyril,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Augustine,</ns0:hi> and some modern Interpreters understand it. Or 2. as a Mediator sent from the Father, so he is greater than I. Or 3. In respect of my present state, while I am here in the form of a servant<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and in my state of <ns0:hi>humiliation,</ns0:hi> which seemeth to be the best in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpretation, if we consider the words before; <ns0:hi>You would rejoice, because I say unto you, I go unto my Father</ns0:hi>: for the true reason of that joy must have been, because Christ in his glorious state of Exaltation, would be much more happy than he had been in his state of Humiliation, while he was exposed to the scoffs, reproaches, and injuries of men, the temptations of Satan, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13.19.</ns0:note> now I have told you before it come to pass, that when it is come to pass, ye might believe <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Evils that surprize us are always the most heavy, and load our spirits (saith our Saviour); before these things come to pass, I have given you notice of them, that when you see them come to pass, you might not be overwhelmed with sorrow, and trouble, to the hinderance of your faith in me; but understanding that I have told you the truth, before the thing come to pass, you may be assured that I am not meer man, but truly God, and receive, and imbrace me, and rest upon me as your Saviour.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 Hereafter I will not talk much with you <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">I shall not have much time hereafter to reveal my mind to you, my suffering is very near, the Devil who is the Prince of this World, <ns0:hi>Chap</ns0:hi> 12.31. (see the notes there) <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 16.11. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 6.12. He cometh by the evil Angels, or rather by vile and wicked men, as his instruments: <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> and the Souldiers. He doth not say wherefore he came, but it is ea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sily understood:</ns0:note>; for the prince of this world cometh <ns0:hi>a,</ns0:hi> and hath no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing in me <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">and he hath nothing in me that he can justly fault, and take advantage against me, for he findeth no guilt in me, to give him any advantage against me; I shall die as an innocent person, and be cut off, but not for my self, (as it was Prophecied of the <ns0:hi>Messiah, Dan.</ns0:hi> 9.26) but (as it is there <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 24.) <ns0:hi>to finish transgression, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting Righteousness.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 But that the world may know that I love the Father: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

So as it is most probable, that the discourses in the two next Chapters were as they went along in the way to <ns0:hi>Mount Olivet.</ns0:hi> In this discourse our Saviour hath most applied himself to relieve his Disciples upon their disturbance, for their want of our Saviours bodily presence.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
